utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I ask the Registrar to call out the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-T, Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi and Mr. Vos for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My name is Mr. Toma Fila, I appear with Ms. Lopicic and Mr. Petrovic in the Defence of my client, Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you hear me? Before we start, let me tell Mr. Fila that I have put in place all the necessary measures for the granting of safe conduct. I read your request which was filed yesterday. The order also covers the last witness -- there are four. I was wondering what sort of protective measures you were asking for, for those four witnesses. I understand you were asking for voice and face distortion, but I assume you are not asking for a pseudonym because you have already mentioned in court their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the day before yesterday I was informed that they are asking for safe conduct. I do not know what they shall be asking by Monday. If they asked for pseudonyms, then I hope the Prosecutor will agree, because this is a joint problem. People hear something today, then they tell somebody else something, and had I not asked for safe conduct for (redacted), I would not have had to ask for anybody else, but they hear that one person has safe conduct status and so they ask for it themselves, so I do apologise for complicating your life in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to the granting of these protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, we do not have any objection. I just make an observation and that is; it is not only in this case but a number of cases, there is a danger -- we do not take objection because we want the Defence to be able to present their evidence and we do not want to see any obstruction to that and we want to see that happen as effectively as possible. It is a concern, though, that this is becoming very prevalent in a lot of cases. It does eventually impact on the public nature of the trials. I do not think it is a matter we can do anything about now, but it is a concern. Certainly, if Mr. Fila says it is necessary in order to have the evidence, then we do not object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will see, depending on what Mr. Fila tells us, whether in addition to the distortion of voice and face, we also need to give them pseudonyms -- you will let us know, maybe even on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I will, quite definitely and I once again apologise to both you and Mr. Niemann. It is not up to me, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We may now proceed with the cross-examination. IVAN CUKALOVIC:

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Overnight we have considered the evidence of Dr. Cukalovic and we consider his evidence is more in the type of an amicus type statement. We will deal with it by way of submission at the end of the day, so we have no cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any re-examination by Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I do not have any additional questions. I would just like to ask you to show the evidence to the witness that the Prosecutor submitted at the request of the court. They are documents which are allegedly of an international character signed by Croatia, and I would like you to tell the witness of these documents so that he knows what they are about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Which documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I do not know the number of the exhibit -- 190-something. It was given yesterday. It is the agreement between the republics. They were submitted as evidence for a Memorandum of Understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We received from the Prosecutor two sets of documents, to the best of my recollection. One set of documents embraced documents relating to agreements sponsored by the ICRC, and then a document from the UN stating the date of secession of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am a little puzzled by all this. If Mr. Fila wants to show the witness something, he is quite welcome to do so, but he does not need to do so in the course of the proceedings. I do not follow what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, are you keen to have some sort of assessment by the witness of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, so that the witness can say whether he has come across these documents working in international law so he knows what the documents are about, yes, that is what it is all about, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution exhibit 192.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might I ask, Mr. Fila, if this is re-examination or a continuation of evidence-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We thought we should be rather flexible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I expected the Prosecutor to ask something. I could not have envisaged the fact that Mr. Niemann would not be asking anything. I just thought that the Prosecution would have some questions to ask, that is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You were taken by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution exhibit 176.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you tell us what it is that you are holding there, what document you have before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a convention which the Republic of Croatia signed in May 1992, and it states that it will be valid as of 8 October 1991. It is not an ordinary document. We are not talking about giving recognition to the Republic of Croatia here, but it is a retroactive effect of international agreements, so these are two notions which are quite different. What the document states and the date that it comes into force is 8 October 1991, therefore, it is a retroactive document. From the viewpoint of international law, when we come to the question of Croat recognition, this, in fact, does not mean anything at all. In all these Acts, the only thing is that that the date 8 October is mentioned on the basis of the report by the Badinter Commission, which is not binding, which is contradictory, and, after one month, he, in fact, overruled himself -- negated himself. I think that this kind of situation was best explained was best explained by Professor Baladero Pagleri. In cases of this kind, we are not dealing with legal recognition. Therefore, if an agreement stipulates that it will have a retroactive effect, and if by this you wish to demonstrate that Croatia was a State on that particular 8 October, Professor Baladero Pagleri distinguishes between recognition, which has only a political importance, and recognition which has a legal effect. Therefore, for the recognition of a State to be legally valid, the State must fulfil certain criteria which we enumerated yesterday, that it have a territory, a population, and sovereign Government. Croatia, on 8 October, did not have any one of these three elements. Where are the key criteria -- active and passive diplomatic offices. With whom did Croatia have diplomatic relations at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object to this evidence as repetition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. We apply the principle Euro novat curiae. We are expected to know international law in particular, and then what you are saying is repetitive, so you already stated your position yesterday. Mr. Fila, do you have other questions, or can we move on to our next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The next witness will be here at 9 o'clock. We did not know that there would be no further cross-examination. Would you please just assess each of these exhibits without repeating what you said yesterday, because the Prosecutor is quite right, you cannot repeat what you have already said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was just explaining what I failed, perhaps, to mention yesterday. The second document relates to the respect of humanitarian principles and it is an agreement between six signatories. This document as an act of recognition once again does not mean a thing. There are hundreds of Acts of this kind. It was signed by Russia with Chechnya and (INAUDIBLE) and none of these three became a State in its own right. They are just agreements which are reached in critical moments to regulate a given situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the case in the Philippines, for example, as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Philippines, the situation was somewhat different. An agreement there was signed between the legal Government of Corazon Aquino and the rebels similar to this one, once again in order to regulate a concrete situation. Furthermore, the Memorandum on Agreement in Geneva on 27 November 1991, once again, a contradiction here, if you please. If Croatia existed as a State on 8 October, how come then that, on 27 November, a Memorandum of Agreement is signed and it was signed by the representative of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is to say, the Federal Minister? Therefore, Yugoslavia at that point was the subject of international law, Yugoslavia's subjectivity is not proved, it is understood -- the subjectivity of Croatia was to be proved. The fact that the signatory on this document was the representative of Yugoslavia demonstrates that Yugoslavia existed more than one month after that alleged recognition of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at the following document -- it is notification of Switzerland--

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we are, once again, the convention, the agreement, which was signed on 16 December 1991. As the first signatory, we have the representative of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Therefore, if Croatia existed, then Yugoslavia no longer existed. On one territory you cannot have the existence of two independent and sovereign States. Let us go on. Finally, an agreement on the establishment of a protected zone around Osijek. That is quite normal, documents of this kind are signed to protect a given zone -- it does not mean international recognition. Then we come to 27 December 1991, once again the signatory is a representative of the Ministry for Health, Labour and Social Welfare, Ljiljana Stojanovic at the first signatory. Those are my comments. I think the situation is quite clear there from the aspects of international law .

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. Cukalovic, do any of these documents which you have seen before you, can any of them be considered agreements concluded between two or more sovereign countries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to prove this, you would have to prove previously the fact that Croatia existed as a State at that particular moment. None of the arguments which we have put forward indicate a conclusion of this kind except Badinter's report, who negated itself one month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like to thank your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Since we have 10 minutes, if the Prosecutor has no questions, I may ask a question. I was not intending to ask any questions, but we can spend the next 10 minutes discussing this particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise, once again, but I would like to ask Mr. Niemann to tell me in advance when he has no further questions so I can bring the witnesses in earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yesterday, we discussed the question of the legal status of the so-called Serb District of Slavonia, Baranja and Srem under constitutional law. May I ask you: how would you characterise the Government of the Serb District of Slavonia, Baranja and Srem from the viewpoint of international law? First of all, is it correct that the area covered by the Serb district is in Croatia only, or does it also embrace some parts of the Serb territory? I looked up the map yesterday and I saw that the word "Srem" is across the border. So two questions -- the geographical extension of this particular district and its status under public international law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as geography is concerned, there is Eastern and Western Srem. One is in the territory of Yugoslavia, and the second part is on Croat territory, so this district does not encompass the territory of the Federal Republic of Serbia, it does not. This area, which has remained the last oasis where there are still some Serbs living in the territory, does not encompass the territory of the Republic of Serbia. The status of the Government, which was set up on this territory, should be determined in keeping with the war operations which were waged at the time. Its status depends on whether or not they control part of the territory, whether or not they had any means of recognition and identification and whether or not they adhered to the provisions of war law. As on that particular territory, organs were set up of the so-called Republic of Serbia and Krajina, they had all the prerogatives of being recognised as a warring party, that is to say, they had -- they were led by a responsible Government, responsible individuals; they had a certain identification and it was the emblem of the Republic of Serbia and Krajina and they had certain military rules and regulations, which showed that they recognised and respected the divisions in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But I think I read somewhere that the so-called Republic of Serbia and Krajina, as you called it, succeeded the establishment of the Serb district of Slavonia, Baranja and Srem. I understand that, when the Republic of Serbia and Krajina was set up, for instance, Mr. Dokmanovic was no longer a Minister of Agriculture of the so-called Serb district of Slavonia. So I thought, but I may be wrong, that the Serb district of Slavonia, Baranja and Srem and the relevant Government was set up probably around September 1991. Then, towards the end of 1991, when the Serb Republic of Krajina was set up, the district of Slavonia and Baranja was dismantled, so, therefore, I thought it was this so-called district and the corresponding Government was a sort of short-lived entity on Croat territory, so my question was therefore, how would you characterise -- if it is correct what I am saying, but I may be wrong -- this particular Government on the territory of Croatia, which lasted only a few months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is quite certain is that that territory had nothing to do with Yugoslav territory and, as far as how we would define that Government, I have already said it was established only as a Defence on the part of the Serb people of a possible Croat terror, namely, what happened in 1941 remained deeply imbedded in the consciousness of the Serb people, and the people there just organised themselves, and according to international war law it is permissible for the population of a particular area to organise itself in the case of a possible massacre, terror and the like. So, this is a region which organised itself with the basic aim of protecting itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But if we proceed on the assumption -- which has been advocated by Mr. Fila as Defence counsel -- that the armed conflict which took place in the area we are referring to between, say, September, October and December 1991, was an internal conflict between Croats, who were rebelling, trying to secede from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, why was it necessary for the Government to be set up for a few months in an area which was under the jurisdiction, if we stick to the thesis of Mr. Fila, of the Federal authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was under the jurisdiction of the Federal authorities, but a lot of crimes can be committed in the space of one month, and they could be unavoidable and, therefore, the population, having the experience that it had, because of the same population in 1941 in only several months were massacred greatly, and it was necessary to organise -- for the population to organise itself in any way they could to try and prevent any possible crimes which I am quite sure would have followed. They did follow, in fact, but thanks to the fact that the people themselves had organised themselves, the Yugoslav People's Army had problems with its commanding officers, and a Croat was at the head of the Yugoslav army, and therefore the people had to organise itself, together with the help of the Yugoslav People's Army, to try and save its integrity and to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You mean not only was it needed for those people to organise themselves not only militarily, from the viewpoint of military structure, but also a Government, with the Minister of Agriculture? Anyway -- thank you. Are there any questions? Is there any objection to the witness being released? No objection. Thank you, Professor Cukalovic for giving testimony, you may now be released. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The next witness has arrived a little earlier, luckily. SLAVKO GAVRILOVIC.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I will just have to explain something both to you and to Mr. Niemann. Mr. Milan Bulajic, the next expert after Mr. Gavrilovic, he will be coming only on Monday. So, after Gavrilovic, we are going to hear the witness Mr. Milinkovic, who is also there. If we finish Mr. Gavrilovic, we will hear Mr. Milinkovic, so it is just a change in the order -- nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness, may I call up on both parties to try to avoid lengthy questions, and I will also ask the witness not to be too lengthy, because we have received the document and he is going to address questions of the Serbs in Croatia, Slavonia, Dalmatia from the 14th to the 20th century. So it is an historical background. We have already heard a lot of information and evidence about the historical background. I think we should focus, as much as possible, on the legal issues and the factual issues relating to the accused. So, let us avoid entering into domains which, in a way, are extraneous to our matter. I would like, therefore, to call upon, in particular, Mr. Fila to try to confine himself to a few questions and relevant questions. We are not interested in the historical background, the sociological or psychological background. As a court of law, we have to pass judgement on the facts and the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fully agree with you. Everything that I am doing now is what Mr. Wheeler wrote about, and then he was questioned on it. Had the Prosecutor not questioned Mr. Wheeler about the 14th and 15th, and 16th century, et cetera, none of this would have been necessary. That is why we have to have such evidence, based on the knowledge of true experts, not what Mr. Wheeler learned within five years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration, Mr. Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, you may be seated. Examination-in-chief by MR. FILA:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor, do you feel comfortable? Can we begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us briefly about your education and what schools you have completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My education took place in Vinkovci, Sremski Karlovci and Novi Sad. I attended university in Belgrade. I did research in archives, especially in Zagreb, Osijek, Karlovci, Budapest, Vienna and Moscow and local archives throughout the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you were employed until now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, I was employed at the teachers' college in Prizren in Kosmet; then, as the custodian of the military museum in Novi Sad and, after that, I went to teach at the Faculty of Philosophy in Novi Sad, first as an Assistant Professor, and at the end of my career I was a full Professor and, finally, I went to work at the Historical Institute of the Serb Academy of Sciences and Arts, and I was retired there a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you been a member of the Serb Academy of Sciences and Arts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1979.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are still a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you the author of many papers and books on the history of the Yugoslav peoples until the 20th century?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote many studies, reviews, over 450 altogether, and I am the author of some 20 monographs and also of 20 publications dealing with original papers on Serbs in the Austro-Hungarian empire, in the Balkans, especially in Croatia, and also, in particular, for some 20 years, I studied the political and social history of Croatia in the 16th, 17th and 18th and first half of the 19th century.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to have a look at what you will be shown now by the usher? Is that your CV, and is it part of your bibliography? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Marked D28.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All of this is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now please have a look at the next document, which is in the Serb and English languages and could you tell me whether this is your expert opinion? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Defence wishes to have both documents admitted into evidence as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That will be D.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D28 and D29 and D29A, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You have given a detailed expertise and the custom before this court of law is to give brief answers once you have provided detailed expert opinions. I understand that. So I am only going to put a few questions to you so I ask you to give as succinct as possible answers, because this is background material, because the matters dealt with in this trial are far more specific than that. Could you please tell me when the Serbs came to the territory, which is the territory of present day Croatia; how did all this start; et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs started moving in very early -- already in the 6th and 7th century, a group of Slavs came from the Carpathian mountains to the Danube area -- they were not ethnically or nationally differentiated yet. These Slavs came under the rule of the Hungarian State at the end of the 10th and beginning of the 11th century. They were intensive, although the relations changed between the medieval Hungarian State and medieval Serbia, so this relationship was sometimes hostile and sometimes friendly, but, as far as Serbs in Croatia are concerned -- I am referring to what is today Croatia -- I think that the Serbs have a distinct profile as of the 13th century, when the Serb king, Dragutin as the ally and vassal of the Hungarian king, received Srem, Belgrade and Macva to be under his rule. This was the Srem of this side and that side as it was called then, because it was the area north and south of the Sava River. Since this was a feudal ruler and a feudal court, it is quite clear that he did not need clerks, and it was not the Hungarians who were members of the ruling nation and who were very few in this area -- they were not tilling his land, so it was only the local people who were tilling the land, that is to say, belonging to his own nation, his own people and to the same religion as he did. Later, when another Serb ruler, Stevan Lazarevic, who had the title of the despot of Serbia, when he became an ally of the Hungarians and a vassal of the Hungarian king, at the very beginning of the 15th century, he received Belgrade and Northern Serbia, which then fell under his rule. So this population, which was first proto Serb and then Serbia, received strong support from Belgrade, which stood near Srem and then the tragic battle of Kosovo took place and finally, in 1459, Serbia finally fell under the Turks. Then, this great migration movement continued from the south to the north, so the Serbs came to this Penonian Carpathian area, Banat more specifically and then gradually other regions as well, and at the beginning of the 16th century, they moved in to Slavonia in larger numbers as they were fleeing from the Turks, or they were brought in by force by the Turks, who one could say started with the ethnic cleansing in the Balkans, because they used to move entire populations from one area to another -- even areas that were very distant, for example, Serbs from Snrdrevo and all the way to Istanbul and Serbs from Herzegovina from the old Raska State to the western part of Bosnia and to central Slavonia. This was done constantly. The first Serb traces in Northern Dalmatia date back to a period which even preceded that. This is related to very important monasteries, if they still exist today -- Serb monasteries, Krupa and -- I am sorry, I just to recall the name exactly -- two important Serb monasteries, at any rate that were founded at the time when the sister of the Serb emperor, Dusan, Serbia's most important medieval ruler, who was married to Mladen Subic III, there, in that central Dalmatian area, because she got married there, and she moved there, and from a religious point of view, the court of the Subices was tolerant, so she was allowed to bring in Orthodox monks, and to establish the first Orthodox churches. That is when these two most important Serb monasteries in north Dalmatia were founded, that is to say, that all of this took place in the mid 14th century. Later, more and more Serbs came to Dalmatia during the Turkish invasion, because the population fled. Part of them went to the Adriatic coast and the islands and other parts of the population went into the mountains towards west Bosnia, to the Una River, and for a certain period of time, while the Croat and Austro-Hungarian borders were the Kupa River and then they went all the way up to the Kupa River, so the Serbs came to this area as Turkish rayah, the subjects of Turkish Lords. They belonged to the Turkish feudal system. Before that, the Turks had totally plundered and devastated the areas that they had conquered before that, so the Turks needed to have an organised area, and so, in addition to the army, they needed a people who would be working for them -- the so-called rayah, they were Christian Serbs predominantly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us move briefly to the military Krajina -- we are going to skip over two or three centuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the Serbs first came to western Bosnia, and then to Hungary to Urad and Komokah, they came into contact with other Christian peoples, with Croat feudal lords, who were at the frontier, that is, on the remains of the Croat kingdom, so their forces were very weak, so it is the court in Vienna that took over the defence line against the Turks -- one would call it the Ministry of Defence today, first in Graz and then in Vienna -- and the royal captains and the royal generals asked the Serbs, who were under Turkish rule, to come over to the Christian side, because they were Christians themselves, because it was their wish, too, to defend the borders of the Austrian empire and partly Croatia, vis-à-vis the Turkish empire, so there was an agreement, either in writing or an oral agreement with smaller or larger groups, and, finally, real agreements were signed between the Serb community and the Austrian royal authorities and, ultimately, the court in Vienna itself, which gave certain benefits to the Serbs, so that, as soldier peasants, they would defend the frontiers. The Croat lords wanted them to be peasants first and then soldiers, and soldiers only if necessary, so they would till their lands, but the royal authorities insisted that they should be soldiers first and foremost, and only then peasants, as much as necessary, that is to say, so they could feed themselves. Practically all the Serbs accepted this position of the court in Vienna and of the Emperor's generals, because this meant they could exist as free men. They would be free of paying taxes, and their only obligation would be to do their army service, and, of course, to be faithful throughout their lives to their ruler and at that time and in the centuries that followed, they never betrayed them -- never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the Krajina benefits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Krajina benefits were the following: first of all, they were free men, free peasants. They did not have to pay any kind of taxes -- none whatsoever -- and, at that time, that was an exceptional privilege -- an exceptional privilege, indeed. And, also, there was tacit recognition of their right to profess their own religion, the Orthodox religion. Also, they had all elements of local self-government and even beyond that, primarily through the so-called Vlach or Serb statutes that the Vienna gave the Serbs in 1630 and, three years before that, it recognised the right to ownership, the right to property, to all that land where the Krajina borders moved into in the 16th and 17th centuries, and this meant that, from a territorial point of view, the military Krajina, the Vojna Krajina, was a distinct part of that area as opposed to Dalmatia, Srem, et cetera. Later on, in 1690, when the patriarch Carnojevic led the Serbs and their great migration from the south to the north, the Serbs received a different status, even stronger than this. They got very broad privileges especially for that time, with the following key point -- the freedom of religion and religious and secular power of the Serb patriarch over the Serb Orthodox people and, also, not only over the Serbs but also the Vlachs, the Cincar -- all of those who were Orthodox. This was later the metropolitan of Karlovski and at the insistence of patriarch Carnojevic and according to the wishes of the entire Serb population in the kingdom, the court in Vienna recognised the Serbs as Pascianica, or Serbica-Pascianica-Illyrica and these privileges were extended to partes adnexae, also to Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia. In that way, if we look at this first stratum of privileges, that is of the Krajina (INAUDIBLE) and then this went further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an academician, you now moved on to the Illyrian movement, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. It came into being of the first half of the 19th century, as a resistance movement of the younger generation of Croat intellectuals and part of the Croat citizenry and also some of the lower Catholic clergy against Hungarian domination, supremacy, and their persistent efforts to assimilate all non Hungarians as they extended the use of the Hungarian language into schools, the administration and overall life in the area. First, the Croat nobility resisted this, but inconsistently and weakly and without a proper organisation. Then it is the citizenry who took this over. The bourgeoisie was mostly educated in Graz, Vienna and Northern Italy and they already had the seed of European liberalism imbued in them. The Illyrian movement, from a religious point of view, was very tolerant and actually they opened the door for the Serbs to Croat political life. Before that, the Serbs were very important from an economic and military point of view, that is to say, the defence of the remains of Croatia, the defence of the Austro-Hungarian empire, because they were merchants, together with the Cincars in this entire Croat/Slavonian/Hungarian area all the way up to Karlovac, Trieste, Rijeka, Karlobag, Srem. Another thing is important, because they were Orthodox, and especially because they did not have a strong nobility, they were excluded from political life. After all, political life at that time was restricted only to the populous, to the nobility -- not all the people -- so everybody else was excluded from politics but now the Illyrian movement opened the door to Serbs to get into political life, to public life and the Serbs understood this and through their intelligentsia and through there merchants --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please slow down, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, and this way they came into Croat political and social life and gave an important contribution to it. I am only going to mention one thing. For example, money affairs in the Slavic south -- the first savings bank in Zagreb was opened by the Serb, Anastas Popovic -- this was a Croat savings bank -- in 1847 and he introduced the Serbo-Croat or Croat-Serb, or as they even then called it, the Yugoslav language, into commerce, which was so important for the psychological situation in Croatia. The Serbs were very agile in the press of the Illyrian movement, especially with Utjesenovic, Ostrozinski and Makso Prica. The Serbs helped the inception of all institutions in Croatia, like the Matica. I have to refer to the fact that the major contributor for the founding of Matica Hrvatska was an ex prince of Serbia, Milos Obrenovic, or rather, his son, Mihajlo. He contributed 2,000 foreign silver coins, whereas the well-known Draskovic family and others only gave 200 or 500 Florins altogether, so this is a figure that can be found in the first history of the Matica, but it is no longer there in the second edition of the history of the Matica, although it was published in Tito's time, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, can we now move on to another important thing? When did the SABOR decision come on the equality of the Serbo Croat language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1840, in the SABOR, there were 52 Serbs, that is, the Croat Parliament. There were never as many Serbs in the Croat SABOR after that, which testifies to the fact that they were important citizens and that they were elected not only by the Serbs but that they were also elected by the Catholics. Slavonians -- Croats, in general. As the Croat SABOR or Assembly accepted and sanctioned the alliance between Vojvodina Srpska proclaimed at the May assembly of the 13th of May b1848, with Srem as a component part -- and I underline this -- a component part, the SABOR accepted this and thereby sanctioned at the most lofty place the alliance and their political unity. In terminology, the language was referred to as "our language". It was rarely referred to as the "Croat language" and even less the "Serb language". It was referred to as "our language" because the integration of the South Slavs was the goal to be achieved. After the breakdown of the revolution and the absolutist period in 1861, there was a renewal of the political and Party life and parliamentarism in the country, and after a lot of trials and tribulations, in 1867 the Croat Parliament met and it was already confronted with the Austro-Hungarian agreement in 1867, according to which there was a dual organisation of the Habsburg monarchy. The Croat politicians were afraid of what was happening and, therefore, they sought an ally, and they had an ally previously in the Serb people -- the Serbs in Croatia and the Serbs in Vojvodina and the Serbs in Hungary and, at the time, the Croat Parliament brought in a clear-cut declaration on the equality of the Serbs and Croats. They accepted the Serb people as a separate people -- a separate nation. Today we would call this a constitutional nation, titular nation, and the language that was used, instead of saying "our language" or the "Yugoslav language" was declared as the "Croat language" or the "Serb language", or the "Serb and Croat language".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now move on to the question of Pravastvo; what do we mean by "Pravastvo"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pravastvo was an ideology, a movement, which was born in Croatia with the rebirth of constitutional life but which came to full expression with the father of the homeland Ante Starcevic. Without entering into the controversy surrounding the personality of Ante Starcevic, I would like to emphasise the following -- together with Elgen Kvaternik and before them with General (INAUDIBLE) was the creator of a genocidal racist theory, which was later to be put into practice in Croatia. The basic thesis is in the following -- Croatia is a unified country, should be in its historical frontiers, somewhere from the Alps, stretching from the Alps to the Black Sea; the Serbs as a peoples do not exist; those who call themselves "Serbs" are in fact -- their roots are Croats -- are Croat. They are just part of the Croat nation, which, their religion tried, as Starcevic said and the people who thought like him, to separate them from the uniform corps of the Croat people. Starcevic went even further and even said that Serb medieval rulers were Croat rulers. This was complete nonsense and the leading individual of Croatia's political life at the time found this ludicrous -- Josip (INAUDIBLE) was among them, and leading historians, Kukuljivic and Franjo Racki. However, this was something that was insisted upon. The Serbs were proclaimed to be (INAUDIBLE) Cincars, Byzantines non brothers, non brothers, and somebody to be destroyed with an axe -- as a mass without any physiognomy, as a people according to Starcevic -- they only merit the axe. This ideology was echoed in the petty bourgeois community of Croatia, first and foremost in the towns, particularly in Zagreb as well in the provinces. This ideology because an instrument of the political Party, the Croat Party of Rights, which was set up to be differentiated from the Croat National Party, People's Party, and the Independent Party later on and the Unionist Party later on and this Party was headed by Ante Starcevic himself and Elgen Kvaternik until the Rakovic rebellion against the Habsburg authorities, and it is interesting to note that the protagonists of that rebellion were the Serbs, because they were in the region, with (INAUDIBLE) at the head as the perpetrator of Kvaternik's rebellion. At the end of the century, this Pravastvo ideology after Starcevic's death was a weapon for Josip Frank, an exponent of the imperialist section of the Austrian court, considered the Vienna court, that after the glorious liberation struggle of the Italian peoples ousted and after the defeats with Prussia, that it needed to be directed towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Balkans and, ultimately, in order to dominate the Balkans which, at the same time, meant when speaking about the Kingdom of Serbia, its strategic encirclement and to absorb it within the monarchy or to destroy it as a State. Everything that Starcevic and Kvaternik proclaimed became his programme in one of the most brutal forms. This was implemented, translated into practice and this resulted in a series of pogroms over the Serb population in 1892, 1895, 1899 and especially in 1909, when a mass under the slogans of the Party when they said "Death to the Serbs" attacked Serb institutions in Zagreb, attacked the banks, the church, the private houses -- there was bestial conduct for three days and everything was destroyed. Although the Serbs at the time showed full loyalty to the State embodied not in the Croat Parliament but in the Habsburg dynasty and in the court at Vienna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we now pass on to the First World War and the London Agreement of 1915; what was offered Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbia, as is common knowledge, after the assassination in Sarajevo, for which the Government was not responsible, was involved in a war, a terrible war, for which it was not prepared, either militarily or psychologically, ideologically. The country was completely exhausted after the two Balkan wars and it was considered that the greatest part of the national goals had been achieved, because, according to the basic document of the Serb national policy, Ilija Garasanin in 1844, the Serb policy was to have been devoted and was, in fact, devoted to the Balkans -- it was a Balkan policy, and if you study Garasanin, who was attacked so much, you can see that, in fact, the kingdom of Croatia and Dalmatia and the Habsburg empire was hardly mentioned. The basic idea of Garasanin and Serb policy was to liberate the Serb people in the Balkans and to create an alliance of the Balkan people in order for the eastern question to be solved on the basis of nationality with the Balkan peoples as actors. This could only be done by a Balkan alliance which was created on two counts during (INAUDIBLE) and once again in 1912, when it became effective and was realised through the Balkan wars and the liberation of the greatest portion of the Balkans from Turkish domination, including the Serbs, including the Greeks and including the Bulgarians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now move on to the 1915 London Treaty; what is offered to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Serbia entered the war and, first of all, its war goal was to defend its own territory and to retain what it had gained by 1914. However, a portion of the Croat intellectuals from Serbia, Bosnia, some Serbs from Vojvodina and Bosnia, left the Habsburg monarchy, they emigrated, and led by Ante Trumbic and Franjo Supilo, the representatives of the Dalmatian stream in the political life of Croatia created a so-called Yugoslav board. This board or committee was supported by the Serb Government and it was to be a sort of agent of the Government, to propagate its political goals, war goals, with the western countries. At that time, there were negotiations between Italy and the forces of the Entente and these Entente forces, with the London pact in 1915, promised part of the Adriatic coast on the South Slav side and to Serbia, very favourable frontiers, in which the greatest portion of the Serb people would be incorporated. Part of the people who would not be included in this extended Serbia, would remain under the power and authority of the Italians in Northern Dalmatia and Lika, whereas the other portion would remain in the trinomial kingdom of Austria and they did not know what their fate would be, whether this would be Croatia or would it be part of the Habsburg monarchy or the Hungarian monarchy -- this was still a debatable question. The Serb Government, under pressure from the Yugoslav board, a council, and led by its intellectuals, refused this, and thus lost a wonderful chance of being an ally to the great Italian people -- very close to the Serb people who were linked by the liberation struggle through Garibaldi, Mussolini and so on and so forth, and the policy of alliance between Italy and Serbia that existed, the Italian and Serb people that existed and to overthrow Habsburg power and authority. When Italy became free, it had every interest in maintaining good and friendly relations with the peoples in the Balkans, especially with the Serb people. This renouncing of the London Treaty cost the Serbs a great deal. The Serb Government accepted an all-embracing programme of unification within a country of all the South Slav peoples, of course, except the Bulgarians whose historical road was quite separate, and in the linguistic sense was not linked to this other portion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Professor, this offer made on the basis of the London Treaty, was the term "Greater Serbia" used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, "Greater Serbia" is an interpretation in historiography, and as we would say, it is a phrase in Austrian propaganda to stand up against Greater Serbia. Was not Austria a great State? Every State is great in one way or another. Serbia had 4 million, Austria had 56 million and it is nonsense to speak about great Serbism. This concept, this notion, comes from Austria and from Vienna. What we were dealing with was a certain expansion for Serbia, which would encompass, under one roof, within the frameworks of one State, one nation -- an Orthodox nation, of course, in relation and with links to other nations and Ilija Garasanin and Prince Mihajlo showed exceptional tolerance towards the Catholics in Bosnia and even towards the Muslims and they knew that there were no ethnically clean States, that you can only have States with peoples who are mixed, because that is what history did, history mixed all these people up and together and the only road was the road to cooperation or a road to self destruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how did the end of the First World War come about, and how is the joint State set up, what is its name, why did the people join this State?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the war, there was a more intensive relationship between the Yugoslav board and the Serb Government. They did not always see eye to eye as to the Government and organisation of a future State, but the essential point is that, in 1917, a meeting in Corfu was held and the Corfu Declaration was proclaimed between the Serb Government and the Yugoslav Council and on this occasion both sides accepted the following: That is to say, the creation of a uniform State of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and that this State should be a monarchy under the dynasty of the Karadordevices; furthermore, that the State be founded upon the principles which would, in greater detail, be elaborated by a constitutional assembly after the constitution of the State itself. In the final stages of the war, there was a renovation of political and party life, after the death of Emperor Franz Josef and in 1917 and 1918 there was a renewal of political life in the trinomial kingdom and in the SABOR of Croatia -- the Croat Parliament -- and the Croat and Serb or Croat Serb coalition which was set up in 1905, which, at all elections up to 1914, always gained a majority vote and which was therefore legally elected after a period of absence, because the Serb members of the coalition were arrested and interned and the Croats, members of the coalition, were pacified partially and became part of the council. But what happened now was that, with the coalition's return to the Croat Parliament, a particular role was played by its presidency, with Mr. Pribicevic at its head, and now, when the complete disintegration of Austro-Hungary took place, the situation was as follows: the Yugoslav board was a little suppressed from the stage and the Croat Parliament came into the foreground dominated by the Croat Serb coalition headed by Svetozar Pribicevic. This was a concept according to which, within the frameworks of the Habsburg monarchy, first of all, to unify the Slovene peoples -- the Slovenes, the Croats and the Serbs from Vojvodina and the Serbs and Croats, of course, and Muslims in Bosnia, as Bosnia was part and parcel of the Habsburg monarchy and to create a Habsburg Yugoslavia, so to speak, which would negotiate on a footing of equality with the Serb Government in Belgrade. However, the Serbs in Vojvodina, on the basis of a plebiscite, on the basis of a voluntary vote, joined the Kingdom of Serbia -- a decision of 25 November 1918, the representatives of the Serbs in Vojvodina -- the Sokci, the Bunjevci people, the Slovaks and the Germans -- I underline the Germans -- came out in favour of joining Serbia. At the same time, the Bosnian Serbs considered that Serbia was the closest State. In Montenegro we had the conjoining of the people with the Kingdom of Serbia. So, the position of this so-called Government in Zagreb was weakened considerably and a very significant moment came about, that is to say, the Italian army began to take over the regions -- and we must say this is an historical truth -- which belonged to them according to the London Treaty -- part of Slovenia and Dalmatia. At that time from Slovenia and from Dalmatia pressure was brought to bear in two directions -- on the one hand, the presidency of the Parliament in Zagreb and, on the other hand, the Government in Serbia, urgently, without any conditions, without any negotiations on the future form that the State would take, to unify, to unite, and the Serb army to take up its positions in areas which were jeopardised by the Italians and, once again, Serbia responded to this demand and, once again, pushed Italy back, although it was a military alliance, a war alliance previously, and accepted these offers -- these urgent offers, not to say pressures -- made for unification and then it was merely a technical question, that is to say, a delegation from Zagreb, led by Ante Pavelic, but not the same Ante Pavelic who slaughtered during World War II, but he was a Croat politician of the first half of the 20th century. This delegation was sent to Belgrade and, through a declaration, proposed unification, which the regent at the time and later King Alexander Karadordevic and that was how a trinomial State was set up. It was the kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Would you just tell us before the break, briefly, the genesis of the Ustasha movement, when was it incepted, who its leaders were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you to be succinct? In 10 minutes we will have a coffee break -- can you conclude, Mr. Fila, your examination-in-chief in 10 minutes, or do you need some time after the recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After the break, perhaps I will have one additional question. I think that will do. At any rate, I will take less than an hour and a half and that is what I gave as my envisaged time of questioning. Please bear this in mind, that I did not go beyond any of the hour limits I set for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us briefly, because in 10 minutes we will be taking a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ideological and theoretical routes of the Ustasha movement lie in the ideology of the Croat Party of Rights of Kvaternik and Starcevic. There were certain reasons for the Croats to express a certain degree of dissatisfaction with the unitarian policies of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, although I underline, in all governments of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, in addition to Serbs, Slovenes, who were exceptionally well represented, and Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were also fairly represented in the Parliament and in the Government, there were also Croats -- the first Minister of Foreign Affairs, that is to say, one of the most important ministries in a country, was a Croat -- Ante Trumbic. He was the one who led the Serb delegation, or, rather, who negotiated during the peace negotiations in Versailles and before that and, of course, he particularly bore in mind the western boundaries of the new State -- that was of special importance to him. So, due to the weakness of Serb policies and their lack of caution, especially in terms of the north-eastern border of the State and, even during the dictatorship of king Alexander imposed on 6 January 1929, there were Croats in that same Government, too, even three key ministries were held by Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, but you mentioned Mr. Trumbic, did he represent Yugoslavia at the Conference of Versailles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any problems in connection with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, there were always problems, because the Italians, who were on the side of the Allies during the war, they defended the Treaty of London and the Italians were not happy to see Croats on the Yugoslavia delegation, because they knew they would be fighting primarily for the western borders for Austria, the Adriatic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, please continue about the Ustasha movement, and bear in mind that we have seven minutes only be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, this ideology of the Croat Party of Rights and that meant that there would be no reconciliation with the Serbs. In 1929 after the assassination against Radic in the Parliament and there was undoubtedly growing dissatisfaction, because of this tragic event, Pavelic emigrated and he started rallying together unsatisfied individuals from the ranks of the Croat émigrés in Austria and other countries, those who would follow him. So, relatively quickly, he established a firm foundation for his Ustasha movement. This movement was connected to the European Irredenta, with Hungarian, Bulgarian and other irredentisms -- then they adopted their Statute, their rules, for this nationalist organisation of theirs based on conspiracy with clear objectives -- to struggle against Yugoslavia; to struggle against the Serb people; by resorting to all means; and with the assistance of all possible Allies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his idea regarding the future of the Serbs, if he were to come to power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not conceal this idea, because if we look at the Paroshi period, Serbs were to be expelled from Croatia, they were to be destroyed, or, as they said, they should be reconverted to their original faith, Catholicism, and the Serbs were supposed to be "un-Serbed", as we say today -- they were supposed to become part and parcel of the Croat people, because this entire theory and ideology of the Croat Party of Rights was based on this unfortunate theory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there this idea of three-thirds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not formulated at that early stage. It was contained in the spirit of the Ustasha principles and practice -- the assassination of King Alexander and also the attempt to have an uprising in Lika in 1932, et cetera, but this policy of three-thirds was clearly formulated during the independent State of Croatia, a German Quisling State, and the Doglavonic, the first deputy of Ante Starcevic, was Mile Budak, an important writer. He said that one-third of the Serbs should be converted to Catholicism, another third should be moved out, and a third should be exterminated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, may we conclude by saying that this principle was applied during this independent State of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, absolutely, in a way which is unrivalled in world history, and it superseded, by far, the methods of Ghengis Khan and Tamurlaine by their cruelty. In this text, in this expert opinion that I have submitted, I think that I tellingly demonstrated what these methods were and what the degree of bestiality was -- not cruelty -- bestiality that was applied towards a people who had no leaders, who were peasants. What would a Serb from Kozara be blamed for, an illiterate person, or a Serb from the hills of Slavonia who had hardly seen a town, who hardly knew how to cross himself, but he knew that he was a Serb and he was an Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the consequences were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the consequences were Jazenovac, Jadovno, Tenje, Koprivnica, Mitrovica -- practically every town had a concentration camp in its vicinity. At that time, I was a pupil in the Vinkovci secondary school -- I had completed sixth grade then. Under the Ustasha state, I was a secondary school pupil. I knew about this; I heard about this; I had seen for myself Ustasha ideology in the Vinkovci secondary school, that is to say, in Slavonia, and then during the occupation I suffered a lot of what my people had suffered. In a small village near Vinkovski, it was either 20 or 24 October 1944, I am sorry that I did not remember the exact date, but 64 persons, including my kinsmen, were slaughtered in the most terrible fashion -- their throats were slit, et cetera, they were only half dead when they were buried. A tombstone is still there. Perhaps they are going to destroy it tomorrow, but that is what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I will have another question after the break and you will all be interested in this, because it relates to the memorandum and Mr. Gavrilovic is a member of that Academy of Sciences and Arts involving this memorandum, and Mr. Wheeler talked about this memorandum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We stand in recess until 10.20. (10.00 a.m.). (A short break). (10.25 a.m.).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should like to ask my final question about the famous memorandum. In the meantime, since Mr. Wheeler's testimony to the present day, I have supplied the library with the so-called memorandum of the Serb Academy of Science in English and you can acquaint yourself with the text whenever you like. I should now like to ask the Professor to tell me, briefly, what the memorandum is, how it came into being, is it a text or a draft, how it was published, and so on and so forth, and what the consequences are, who drew it up and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The memorandum was to have been a critical programme design document, which would indicate to the Serb people the situation in which they find themselves and would propose ways and means of getting out of a situation of that kind. However, events took a different direction -- a dramatic direction. Let me say at the outset, however, that the time in which the decision was made to draw up a document of this kind, programme oriented, was the time after Tito's death when the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, which still existed at the time, pledged to follow Tito's road, even after his death and the slogan was "With Tito, after Tito" -- that was the official slogan of the day. However, the Serb people, during Tito's era and in the post-Tito era, were not neglected and their position was tragic and the position of the Republic of Serbia within a Federal State of Yugoslavia. Via two provinces, the province of Kosovo and the province of Vojvodina, the Serb political and therefore Party peaks continuously was disempowered to implement the economic, political and other goals which stood before the country, both before Serbia and the Serb people in that State. We had a strange phenomenon of anti-Serbism where we would expect, at least on the territory of Macedonia, there was the Macedonianisation of everything. None of the Serbs denied the Macedonian Federal State, but, within that State, the Serbs were treated worse than a national minority. What particularly gained expression was the fact that Serb cultural and historical monuments were desecrated and the appropriation of all medieval monasteries built by Serb rulers or the Serb dynasty and Serb military cemeteries during the First World War were violated. Macedonia was once under Turkish power and authority. Slovenia went its own way. It used the mask of Yugoslavia -- the Yugoslav mask, but implementing its profoundly nationalistic policy, particularly in economic policy, but, as I am not an expert in this realm, I do not want to enter into detail, and I do not think that it is necessary at the present moment. In the case of Vojvodina, we had a very strange type of separatism, which had its roots partially in the former Austro-Hungarian monarchy, in which a very insignificant portion of the people, but they were not without influence, they were sorry that the old monarchy had disappeared, and these individuals said that Serbia was waging a unification policy in relation to Vojvodina. In fact, it was a question of a dogmatic stream within the Party -- the Party hard-liners and dogmatists and the vestiges of Stalinism in the political ranks of Vojvodina, both with the Serbs in Vojvodina and the non-Serbs --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, briefly, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me say what happened in Bosnia and Croatia, in two or three sentences. In Bosnia, we have the expression of Islamisation, which was masked beforehand, and this was reflected in the cultural and economic life of Bosnia. As I am better acquainted with the cultural life, let me say the following. The thesis was put forward that the Turkish administration and the Turkish State was not an imperialistic State in which genocide was tolerated and implemented, but that it was almost an ideal community for the peoples of the Balkans. The pressure exerted on Serb intelligentsia was that, one by one, they began to leave, like Vojislav Lubarda, the poet, Gojko Nogo, Palevestra, historian of literature, Slavko Leovac and a whole host of leading Serb intellectuals were forced to leave Sarajevo, because, on the one hand, they were under the direct pressure of the Party organs in which the Serbs as well -- Serbs having no backbone -- people like Todo Kurtovic, Mijatovic and others -- in fact waged a satellite policy, they became satellites and appendages to the Bosnian Islamisation. Let me now say a few words about Croatia. A similar tendency was seen in Croatia. As an historian, let me say the following: In Croat histiography, the books written, Serbs were minimalised or were passed over altogether. In the excellent "History of the Croats" written by Professor Sidak Karaman, Dragovan Sepic and Mirjana Gross, it is stated in the introduction that "the Serbs have been left out". Well, they showed enough consciousness to say that the Serbs have been left out and that a separate history of the Serbs would be written, and so on and so forth. So, everything which in the past was positive was ascribed to only one nation, that is to say, the Croat nation, whereas most of what was negative and which could compromise Croatia in the eyes of Europe was ascribed to the local Serbs, the Serbs living in Croatia. Therefore, endeavours were made to exclude the Serbs; there was silence about the Serbs and they were eliminated and, in this case, part of the Party leadership, which was composed also by Serbs in Croatia, with the well-known Srecko Bijelic and Dusan Dragosavac and others, a policy was waged in complete agreement with the Croatising tendencies, which caused a great discontent among the Serb people and the Serb intelligentsia. Let me mention just one detail. When the leading Slavist and linguist, today's world renowned linguist, academic Pavle Ivic, wrote his brilliant book, "The Serb People and its Language", nobody else -- it was Dragosavac who stood up and attacked Ivic and Serb science as a whole, not only for the linguistic consequences of his book, but what left the realm of linguistics and entered the realm of politics. Therefore, the memorandum was to emerge in a very difficult situation for the Serb people, at least as we, the intellectuals, not to say the leading intellectuals, saw and felt the situation to be. In an atmosphere of this kind, when the Academy of Science was wholly dissatisfied with the policy of the central committee of Serbia and the Government of Serbia and the politics of Serbia within the federation, a decision was taken to create -- let me call it -- a drafting editing group which would draw up a critical review -- a comprehensive critical view of the existing state of affairs, and it proposed the roads towards the future and directions which could serve as a groundwork for the creation of a national Serb programme, as it was the conviction of the Serb intelligentsia that Serbia did not have a national programme and that, as it lacked a true, genuine, national programme, it could not wage a national policy, of course, respecting the fact that we were within the composition of a Federal State, which we did not want to destroy. But, the desire and wish was not excluded to restructure it, to cultivate it and as it had severed links with the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc, to find itself in Europe, the position which it merited and from which it was born and to which it had given so much in the past. The idea was that individual experts, or groups of experts, two or three individuals from the realm of economics, politics, political historiography, art and so on and so forth, should get together and write texts which would be united, and which would be subject to the editing by this editorial group which was set up. It was envisaged -- there were to be six or seven chapters. I followed developments along these lines, although I was not directly involved because I was not living in Belgrade, but was living in Novi Sad in the Vojvodina province, but I attended meetings of the Assembly of the Academy of Science regularly, and, at the time, had this document been completed, once it was presented before the editorial board, it would be sent on to the executive board of the Academy of Science and it was this board --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you. I wonder if you would be so kind to set out, in a few sentences, the gist of this memorandum so we can come to the end of this examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Professor, it was not brought to the editorial council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The essential point to note is that it would have the value of an official document and an official attitude of the Academy of Science, had it been adopted by the Assembly of the Academy of Science, and this never took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say as our first conclusion that it is not an official document of the Academy of Serb Science?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. First of all, because it was never completed and, second, because it never went through all the bodies of the Academy of Science. Therefore, it is just in an uncompleted portion -- an incomplete document, drafted by individuals and groups of citizens within the Academy, members of the Academy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, could you tell us, please, how this uncompleted document went public and the reactions of official Serb policy to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How the memorandum -- that is to say, this document which was conditionally called "the memorandum" -- how it became public remains unclear to the present day -- opinions differ. It seems that what happened, and I as a member of the Academy heard this -- and this is the most probable explanation -- that the late professor, the Professor of the Faculty of Law, Jovan Dordevic, received the first part of this memorandum which was drafted, and it was sent to him to review it from a legal aspect, in the meantime, waiting for other texts. But, allegedly, his son-in-law -- I do not remember if his name was Jovan Jovanovic, took the text from his writing table, had it copied and sent it to the papers and, behind this act, it is considered that it was the head of internal security, the Slovene, Stane Dolanc, who was responsible for this act, with the clear goal of coming by material which could compromise the Serb Government and the Serb central committee, which had started this struggle for a constitutional revision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, can we say, therefore, that the document saw the light of day without authorisation from the Academy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the last question: they do not know, professors, names like Dolanc and so on. They mean nothing to the members of the Tribunal, so let us have a look at the attitude of official Serb policy towards the memorandum -- the President was Milosevic; is that correct? What did the Government have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivan Stambolic was President at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the official attitude of Serb policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milosevic was at the head of the Party forum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was this memorandum received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Government of Serbia and Central Committee of Serbia received the memorandum, as they said, as a "knife in the back". They could not come to terms with it. They could not come to terms with the fact that somebody outside their ranks, particularly outside the ranks of the Party, and most of the academics were not Party members, how could they think with their own heads and take a step which would be contrary to the Government -- opposed to the Government -- showing the Government and the central committee as incapable individuals, disoriented leadership, which was losing its footing amongst its own people and the Academy reacted drastically. First of all, there was a witch hunt, a campaign, in the press against the Academy of Science, against individuals, and against the Academy as an institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your financial resources withheld?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they went as far as saying that there was the danger that the Academy be dissolved, and that new elections in the Academy be held, because the regime thought that it would frighten the academics and that a small group of academics, 17 members in all, I do not know whether or not this is true but I do know, and it was difficult for me to say this -- my Professor, where I did my Ph.D., whose assistant I was, he was a one time Minister (INAUDIBLE) was one of these individuals, who together with Pavlesavic and others was to have undermined the assembly of the Academy, and was to bring about a vote of no confidence to the executive board of the time and, quite simply, to turn the clock back, and then to have re-elections take place in the spirit and intentions of the Government and the Central Committee of Serbia, to select the people they wanted to have in the Academy. Furthermore, the Academy, for several months, all financial resources were withheld -- financial resources which belonged to the Academy by law -- the Academy is a not a chorus or a choir -- only two or three institutions were guaranteed their position by law -- first of all, the Serb Academy of Science and Arts and the Matica Hrvatska organisation. The Government and Central Committee overruled this view and they refused to finance the Academy. They said that the academics would not be receiving part of their salaries and we just laughed, because we were not in the Academy for a measly supplement of less than 100 marks. Furthermore, systematically, they wanted to separate the administration of the Academy from its members and for several months nobody received their salary in the Academy, but from the cleaning women right up to the Secretary-General, everybody stood behind the academics themselves, and then, from some reserve funds, which were set aside for scientific research, we managed to guarantee the administrators their salaries and we went to the Assembly, which was tied up with the centenary celebrations of the Academy. The Academy had already sent out invitations to 150 addresses throughout the world -- kindred Academies throughout this world, and this was to have been a general assembly, a great manifestation to celebrate the centenary. However, as the Academy lacked funds, our colleagues and delegations from all over the world were not able to come, because we were not able to finance them, but, instead of them, we had the representatives of practically all the embassies ranging from the Japanese straight through to all the others, and they attended the Assembly, which was a very lively one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to stop you, but I wonder whether you could refrain from going into so many details. Mr. Fila, are you through?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am not through -- yes, I have finished. I am not drawing to an end, I have reached the end. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the Prosecutor has any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have a number of questions. These relate mainly to the written submission. It deals primarily with the more recent history.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Professor, you have indicated that you were a member of this Serb Academy of Arts and Science. Would it be fair to say the Academy has had some degree of influence in Serbia and among Serbs outside of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Academy did not have a major influence by virtue of the fact that it could hardly exist financially, and it was on the margins of all events generally speaking -- you know what communist rule means -- they thought that all wisdom was in the heads of the members of the Central Committee and we were, what, a necessary evil? They tried to tolerate us and nothing more than that, but the very fact that we were a Serb Academy of Sciences and Arts meant that we had some kind of authority -- I would not say influence -- but, you know, in the thinking of the Serbs in Croatia, in Canada and elsewhere, so it is impossible to deny it and why deny it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You have testified today and you have indicated in your curriculum vitae that you suffered quite a bit during the Ustasha period. I do not in any way want to minimise your loss and suffering that you went through, but, with all respect, does this not make it difficult for you to provide a detached, objective analysis of events during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the least. I did suffer during the war, as a pupil who had not even completed secondary school yet, I had only finished 11th grade. I was a pupil in Croatia, in Vinkovski, and I did a lot of my research in Zagreb, in Croatia, and I had wonderful colleagues and friends among Croats, particularly among historians, especially the late Professor Jaroslav Sidak, Igor Karaman,, Mirjana Gross, Ivan Erceg -- well, he is still alive. In my research in Zagreb, I never encountered any impediments of any kind, but I did get into situations which were rather unpleasant. You know, people trusted me, and they knew that I was not a spy of the authorities, that I was not a stool pigeon, that I was a free-thinking intellectual, so they would say things in front of me which they would not say elsewhere. They would express their attitude towards the Serbs in Croatia, towards the authorities and towards the situation in the country as a whole. By profession, by vocation, so to speak, I am a scholar, I am an historian, I apply critical methods sine ira et studio -- this is my life motto. During my scholarly activities, whenever I encounter documents that did not really speak well of the Serb people, I presented them quite freely. I did it even about the leading people during the life of Tito, and I was subjected to critical views, regardless of whether I expressed views about Serbia and Serb hierarchy or Croats, Catholicism, et cetera, so I wish to state that any kind of Party affiliation, nationalist chauvinist association is something that is foreign to the very essence of my being, although I did, indeed in my youth, see Vukovar and Paucje and Virovitica and Pokupoje and Prigorje and Zagorje, where my very own brother was killed, and, regardless of this major tragedy of inconceivable proportions -- inconceivable especially in view of its bestiality, all of this that I witnessed, that I saw -- my best friend, you know, after I was arrested in November 1942, was taken to Jasenovac and he was built into a wall while he was still alive -- alive! But my conscience always prevailed as a scholar -- a Serb scholar who wrote more historical writings about the Croats, the Ruthenians, the Slovaks, the Hungarians, the Cincars, so it is I who did this, Dr. Slavko Gavrilovic, I wrote about all of them more than anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In your written statement, during your discussion of history from the 1300s through to the end of World War II, it is extensively footnoted. In fact, you have 39 footnotes during that period. In the final three pages in which you offer opinions about events of the last 50 years, there appears only one footnote. Does this indicate that there is a lack of scholarly corroboration for the views you are expressing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, scholastic views are not close to my heart -- it is critical views that are close to my heart. Scholastic views are left to the medieval times.
