What you are saying is true -- Academic Gavrilovic is an expert in history from the 16th until the mid 19th century -- that is what I said, and that is what my CV and bibliography speak of. However, I wrote this expert opinion as a whole, so it is quite understandable that the scientific apparatus is dense in the first part, and it is quite the opposite in the second part. The second part does often contain my own personal knowledge, my personal experience, and my knowledge on the basis of literature, which I read from the days when I was a student. Of course, I cannot say that I can meritoriously speak about the most recent period as I can for the period for which I am a true expert, which I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But you have included this period in your expert opinion, which has been submitted to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes and, in addition to these most recent times and these dates, which I had been registering as a citizen, I am prepared to testify on that period, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you feel that it was important to educate Serbs about what happened under the Ustasha Government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. If anything is important about man, it is his memory, it is his history. No matter how much we may minimise the past or suppress the past, it is in us -- it is within our very human beings. How can I not tell my son, "Son, your father went through a Golgotha during the Ustasha Independent State of Croatia, your father was a person who confronted the Ustasha? Very little, the Germans." As you know, history blamed Germans and Italians for the entire war in order to relieve Croats of all responsibility and they should have been held accountable in the first and Second World Wars, so it is impossible to exclude this component of our lives in the education of young people and, also, at the department where I used to teach -- I did not teach recent history I taught a different kind of history -- but this is part of our everyday lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In fact, starting in the late 1980s and into the early 1990s, there were a number of television programmes and documentaries that were shown on Serb television about Jasenovac and the Ustasha period. Do you think this, in any way, contributed to increasing tension among Serbs and further destabilising the situation in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What could we have achieved with the opposite? What did we achieve by having denied our people that for four decades? They did not have a real conception of the immediate past. They did not know how monstrous these crimes were, and these attempts at exterminating an entire people during the Second World War -- this should not be overlooked. We should not live with lies. A background is very important; history is the background of the present day and the present day is the background of the future. The Serbs certainly had some idea of Jasenovac. There was not a single person who did not know about Jasenovac. How could a son and grandson not know about what his father, mother, grandmother and grandfather had gone through? We cannot exclude the family as such. Every Serb in Croatia and elsewhere had heard of Jasenovac and all the suffering. After all, historiography and history text books for secondary schools tried to overlook this, but they could not overlook it completely. It was said, nevertheless that, during the occupation, the Ustasha behaved in a bestial manner in Jasenovac, Jadovno, in the (INAUDIBLE), in Herzegovina, et cetera. It was not really inciting, because these facts were not new for the Serb people; they simply became obvious or rather more obvious to the younger generation now -- not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In your written statement, you say that the Serbs in Croatia had no alternative, but at the last moment, in the places in which they were a majority, to prepare to defend themselves, not to allow themselves to be disarmed and exterminated and even to create their own State, Srpska Krajina. If this was a defensive action by the Serbs, why was it necessary to expel the Croat population from the areas that came under their control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go into that, first and foremost. I am informed about this to the extent that any average citizen is, with the following distinction -- the man in the street reads five different newspapers, for example, and I read only one daily newspaper because I have so many things I want to do as a scholar. I could not really remember your entire question. Could you please repeat the second part of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well. In your written submission, you say, to paraphrase, that the Serbs, in order to defend themselves in places in which they were a majority, created their own State, Srpska Krajina. I am asking you if this was a defensive action by the Serbs, why was it necessary to expel the Croat populations from those areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not know everything that was happening on the ground, but, as far as I know, there was no systematic expulsion of the Croat population when the Serb Krajina was being established on the basis of the tradition of Serb political life and ethnic development in the former Habsburg monarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour, but I did not find anywhere in the written expert opinion that this witness said it was necessary to expel the Croat population. Could the Prosecutor please read this out? Where it was necessary, what was done to the Croat population, where were they expelled? Please do not put your conclusions or your misconceptions into the mouth of this witness. Where does he say so? Could you please read this out to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: My question was very clear. I read the statement that he made where he said it was a defensive action and then I asked him, if this was a defensive action, why was it necessary to expel the Croat population. At no point did I say that he had --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who told you it was necessary -- whoever said this? How can you claim that this was done? The question was whether it was necessary. Why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Your quote is from the written statement, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you tell us where?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, it is the next to last paragraph in the English translation, on page 6996, which begins with the statement: "In such a situation, the Serbs in Croatia had no alternative --" Again, I quoted that directly; the second time around I did paraphrase it because he said the question was too long. I think that there is ample evidence that the Croat population was expelled from Ilok, from Lovas, from Tovarnik, from (INAUDIBLE), from Vukovar -- from all these areas. I am asking him about facts that are in evidence and asking him to comment, that if this was a defensive action, why was it necessary to expel the Croat population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, your objection is overruled. Please, you may proceed. Could you please answer the question put by the Prosecutor, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, may I say that nowhere in my text, not in a single word do I mention expulsions of Croats. I wrote my text as a general essay, and I did not go into all the events that occurred from the moment when the Serb resistance movement came into being and from the moment when the Serb Krajina was created. I have always believed, and I believe now, that people and experts who are directly involved, or who were directly involved, should speak about this, and I am not one of them, and I state responsibly to you, Sir, that I know how to read, and that nowhere is there a single word or a single formulation of that kind. After all, I said in such a situation the Serbs in Croatia had no alternative but at the last moment, et cetera, et cetera, not to allow themselves to be disarmed and exterminated and even to create their own State, Srpska Krajina -- that is what I said, no more, no less. Perhaps you do have different data, because you have done research of your own and perhaps you have come across various things during this trial, but I cannot speak about it. It was not the objective of this historical analysis of mine to talk about such things. I was supposed to show how this last conflict broke out and what happened during this conflict, I have very little information on that, just like an average citizen -- I know that various things happened and that people lost their lives, like in any war, and this is to no-one's honour, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, may I point out to you before you start with your next question that, as it was very clear from the outset, this court is not really interested in the historical background of the armed conflict, and we are only interested in the facts of the case and the law which must be applied, so therefore let us start from the assumption that this general background is not material. So, if you could be so kind as to confine your questions to the relevant point. I would also call on the witness to be as concise as possible in his replies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If I may address that for the moment. The Defence has maintained that the Serbs in Croatia were defending themselves and that the Yugoslav army became involved only in an effort to protect them and to maintain Yugoslavia. The Prosecution's position has been that the Serbs embarked on an effort to create a Greater Serbia and that, in fact, the Yugoslav army had become a Serb army and this turned into a conflict between the Serbs and the Croats. This witness has made claims to this effect in his written statement, and this is the position that has been put forth by the Defence. We feel that it is necessary to some extent to go into these issues about the creation of this State and what was the intent of the Serbs at the time, so this is where these questions are directed, but I will try to keep it as close to the point as possible. Perhaps, based on the Professor's statements, I can just put a question and maybe we can get around this altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Is what you are saying that, in the period after World War II, the statements that you have included in here are made not as an expert, but as a citizen who observed events and read the newspaper and, if that is the case, perhaps this part of the statement can be withdrawn from evidence and then I would have no further questions on these issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, that would be the gist of it, because I cannot proclaim myself to be an expert in the history of the peoples of the former Yugoslavia, or even present day Yugoslavia in the most recent period, but I was invited to speak here as a witness and I wrote most of this text, especially the first part, on the basis of my own knowledge and research, and on the basis of Serbia, Hungary, Germany and other history and other histiography. In order to speak about this most recent period as an historian, meritoriously, I need documents. I am a scholar. I need a time distance. Even if I were an expert in this period of time in history, I would not have enough facts or sources, so, indeed, as a citizen, and I am not ashamed to say this, as a patriot, too, I knew this. So, that is how, more or less, the milieu that I live in feels and thinks, but, as far as individual facts are concerned, you will have an opportunity to ascertain that during your questioning and hearing of different witnesses. I have seen from the transcript that you have talked to people who can specifically say in such and such a time and such and such a date, but I really cannot do that, and that would be unfair, and it would not do me honour and it would not honour this honourable court if I were to say otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the portion after World War II is being withdrawn as part of the expert submission, I would have no further questions. If, however, it is to be maintained, I think I am obligated to go into the issues as to the issues he raises and the claims he makes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It could still be tendered in evidence, however, with the sort of caveat, namely, that the part after World War II does not reflect the position of a distinguished historian, but simply the views of --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- a citizen. Would you agree, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Absolutely, your Honour. You have probably noted that I did not put a single question from that period in my line of questioning. There is a different expert in that field, that is Professor Bulajic, who you will hear on Monday. I had confined myself to the beginning of the Second World War. I did not mention Jasenovac. I only mentioned the memorandum. I fully accepted this. That is why I did not go into that part of his expertise, otherwise I would have been putting questions along those lines, too, and you did not hear me put a single question on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a man, I spoke about a humane dimension, the suffering of my people, and I am never going to overlook this. I was a participant in all of that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No questions? I assume there is no objection to the witness being released.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, for coming and you may be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We will call upon the next witness. Would you like me to call the next witness now, or are we going to have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, now. (The witness withdrew). MILENKO MILINKOVIC:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, may I ask you to make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Examination-in-chief by MR. PETROVIC:

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milinkovic, would you please tell us whether, on 24 February 1998, you talked to lawyer Miroslav Vasic and did you give Miroslav Vasic a statement. Did you make a statement. Would the usher please show this witness a statement, the English and the Serb original, so that the witness can identify the signature on the document? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I hope you will not speak so fast as Mr. Fila, so the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I shall do my best, but it seems to be our school.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D30, the English translation is D30A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that your statement and your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Would this statement be admitted as D30 or D30A, the English version? Mr. Milinkovic, would you please tell us something about yourself? You are an electronic engineer and an engineer in atomic physics. In the period between 1983 and 1990, you were the Director of the post in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was director of the PTT in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about your work as Director of the Post Telegraph and Telephone company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Vukovar when there were 4,500 telephone lines and over four and a half years there were 28,000 in the municipality of Vukovar. The municipality of Vukovar at the time had about 26,000 households, which means that it had a high degree of development in the telephone service area and I was granted the greatest recognition by the PTT of Croatia and hold an order for labour for my efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political organisation at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was, I was a member of the League of Communists of Croatia, and after it changed its name into the SDP, I was also a member of that Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you a representative in the first parliamentary assembly after the multi-Party elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was elected as a representative of the Council of Municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Would you please tell us something about your political work in that period, that is to say, at the end of the 1980s and the beginning of the 1990s? First of all, I have in mind the beginnings of the transformation of the League of Communists of Croatia into a different political organisation and the overall beginnings of political transformation in Croatia and social transformation as well and I have in mind the 11th congress of Croatia, the Croat Party?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore the 11th congress of the League of Communists of Croatia, when was that meeting held and what happened at that particular congress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was elected as delegate at the 11th congress of the League of Communists of Croatia. It took place, as far as I recall, in 1989. I was in the commission for reform -- there were three commissions -- one was a reform of the economic system. After my presentation within that commission, I took part in the work of the commission for a reform of the political system, but without any intention of presenting a paper before that commission. When, at one particular point, the Chairman concluded the discussion, and proposed that one of the conclusions of the discussion be that the transition to a multi-Party system should take place immediately, I asked for the right to reply, and presented the view that pluralism, which world practice has shown is the most effective way of establishing competitiveness in politics, and the most effective way, but I raised the question of whether we, as a society, were ready for that transformation -- were ready to enter this new form of organisation, especially in view of the fact that there were still national tensions to clear up and, therefore, I proposed that, by using the experience of western Europe in the field, which, after the conclusion that a longer period of time would be necessary for unification and for the dovetailing and harmonisation of all legal and other acts and overcome the barriers in people's minds, that we should do this as well following that model, because we did not have a lot of time -- perhaps only half a year. But that this was the way in which we should proceed. The chairman took note of this and he accepted my reply, but my conclusion was not adopted and although it was not voted on in favour, the conclusion to move to a multi-Party system immediately was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something about the pre-election campaign? The elections took place in the spring of 1990. Could you tell us a little about the pre-election campaign, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of the SDP, certain changes had taken place and for the multi-Party elections we were called the SDP and we organised ourselves for the pre-election campaign. We went to all the local communities in the municipality -- there were about 40 of them, rural and urban ones alike -- and we held our meetings, presenting our Party programme, so that we could win over the electorate. On one occasion, in the village of Lovas, there was a pre-electoral meeting that we organised and I was surprised to see very few people turn up, although practically everybody knew me in that particular village, because I solved the telephone connection problem in that particular village and I held a lot of meetings while we solved this problem of the telephone linking and telephone lines. When the meeting ended, I noticed that the HDZ was having a meeting afterwards. As I did not know who the members of the HDZ were, I decided to stay in the hall, and see. The other members of my Party left for the next meeting but I waited in the hall, waited for the people from the HDZ to turn up, and I saw who the members were -- they were Mercep and the others, because I did not know them beforehand -- I had just seen them, perhaps. I asked to be allowed to stay as a guest, an observer at the meeting, and they accepted this. I sat in the first row -- it was, in fact, a cinema in which we held our meeting which was pack-jammed, there were not enough seats for everybody but nobody sat either to the left or right of me although many people knew me -- nobody dared sit next to me. I accepted this as fear on the part of these people, that they would be labelled as consorting with me. The programme was presented, during the meeting in the usual way. At the end I asked for the floor, and Mercep said that this was not the right time for a discussion. I said that I had no intention of taking part in the discussion, but just to address the meeting as a guest. I went up to the rostrum and I said that I come from another political Party, that I had held other political views, but as a man of goodwill I wanted to address the meeting, and the public before me and all men of goodwill. This led to a round of spontaneous applause and Mercep was very angry, and he did not wait for me to return to my seat, but asked me some questions, so I had to go back up to the rostrum to answer those questions. There were many other questions that were asked on the occasion by people up in the chair, candidates for the HDZ membership and from the audience, so, for practically half the time the meeting lasted, I was at the microphone answering the different questions. I recall one particular individual, and one particular question. They asked me how this new Party of ours, the SDP -- it is an abbreviation for the Party of Democratic Change -- how it wished to settle accounts with its members, that is to say, with the members who were not like-minded. I said that it was a truly democratic Party which did not settle accounts with people -- even if they did not feel as they did and particularly not with their own members, and that, as apart from other parties, it was truly a democratic Party. On that occasion I got to know people from the HDZ for the first time, and, in my desire at the beginnings of political pluralism, I proposed to pool our efforts to the Director of the Agricultural Community, that after the meeting, on their own premises, to organise an improvised round-table discussion. They accepted this idea, and we did have a discussion of this kind. There were some 20 people. I was alone representing the SDP. I had to answer many questions, some of them provocative ones, and at one particular point, a young man -- later he was a deputy in the Municipal Assembly -- when he heard that according to my national affiliation I was always declared -- I always declared myself as a Yugoslav, he asked me, "How is this possible? How can you declare yourself as a Yugoslav?" Because he knows that he is a Croat and therefore he cannot be a Yugoslav by the same token. This was a provocative question. He asked whether I had declared myself as a Yugoslav in my time out function, until I find my identity. I answered, and calmed the others present, that if we were going to discuss a particular issue, then we must know the substance, the background, and that an individual seeks his identity first within the frameworks of his inner self and then from the particular towards the general, he goes via his family, via his environment, via the town he lives in, via the region, the State and Europe, and that I was very sorry to see that he had embarked upon this road only yesterday, that he had left his village yesterday, whereas I had found my identity long ago within the State and that I was now looking for my identity within Europe, to be a citizen of the world in times to come and I must say that I gained the impression that many of them did not understand what I was, in fact, saying. But, at all events, I endeavoured to bridge the gap in our different opinions so that we could avoid what, unfortunately, was to take place later on. I also recall that I intimated that, at the meeting on the following day, in Bogdanovci, that I would like to come to the meeting on the following day, if they agreed to this. They did agree to it and I asked Mr. Mate, who is a Croat by nationality, an ethnic Croat -- he was at one time President of the Executive Council of the Municipal Assembly and he was a member of the SDP as well -- I asked him to go to the meeting with me. He agreed, although I saw that he was not very enthusiastic -- he had probably been told that it would not be a very pleasant meeting. And I suppose that they came to realise that, if I was a guest, they had to treat me as such, and they invited Mr. Glavas to the meeting and I saw him there for the first time, and that there was a euphoric atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us who Mr. Glavas was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I heard from the information media, he was a member of the HDZ , whether he was the HDZ leader in Osijek or not, I am not quite sure, but I heard about him from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, all my attempts to prevail through force of argument and to have a dialogue by political means was absolutely impossible, because of the euphoria that remained amongst the audience and, because Glavas grabbed the microphone, and he started shouting, "This is Croatia. Vote for the HDZ". There were some very provocative questions and insulting questions and I must admit that I had absolutely no chance of setting up a dialogue. After the meeting in Bogdanovci, I never went to any pre-electoral HDZ campaign meetings but went to our own SDP meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Could you just clarify something for us -- the reason you wanted to attend these meetings of what was a competitive political organisation at that time -- a rival political organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that the reason I went to this meeting was because I wanted, and my Party wanted, to establish a political dialogue between parties within the frameworks of a democratic atmosphere, so that this process of democratic elections could be held in a democratic atmosphere and that the different political opinions be resolved parliamentary, that is through political means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when the first multi-Party elections were held in Croatia, what deputies were elected at these elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The elections were held at the beginning of May 1990 and at those elections, apart from the SDP Party, we had the participation of the HDZ, another Party was formed to represent the socialists, but less important ones -- the largest parties were in the SDP areas, the HDZ. As I say, up to that point I did not know the HDZ representative sufficiently well, but as I say, the elections were held, and members elected -- members to the Municipal Assembly, the deputies themselves. About 115 deputy posts were up for election and the representatives for the Croat Parliament -- the SABOR -- were elected and for the socio-political Chamber, one representative for the Chamber of Municipalities, and for these two representatives, the entire voting corps of the municipality -- there were two other Chambers for Associated Labour where the electorate was divided into three parts and each part was to elect its own representative. The elections for the most part, according to the facts that I have at my disposal, regardless of the fact that, at the HDZ meetings, there was this feeling of euphoria, but nonetheless the elections were -- evolved correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What were the results of the elections, both locally and at the Croat Republican level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the local level, the overall results were such that the vast majority of votes, some were around two-thirds, went to the candidates of the SDP Party. They were not all members of the SDP Party actually, but were on the SDP list as prominent individuals in the municipality -- well-known for their efforts in the area -- and, if I am correct, I think only 23 deputy posts were won by the HDZ. As I say, about 115 seats in all. On the other hand, as far as the election of members of the Parliament of Croatia were concerned, in addition to myself, a member of the SDP was also elected from the socio-political Chamber as well as two members from the Associated Labour Chamber and the fifth deputy did not enter the elections as the member of any political Party, so he was an independent candidate, so the HDZ officially did not have a single MP in the Parliament of Croatia from the area of Vukovar. I remember that particular figure. My opposing candidate was a candidate of the HDZ and in the second round of votes I got almost 63 per cent of the vote, which showed that people voted for me then as people and they voted for me as a person -- not as a member of a national or ethnic community, but I had won their confidence as a person. In the Croat Parliament, the voting was as follows: I think there were some 323 seats altogether -- a two-thirds majority almost was won by the members of the HDZ, but the true outcome of the vote in terms of percentage was that about 40 per cent of the vote was won by the HDZ and about 30 per cent of the vote was won by the SDP and I looked at the official reports on the voting in the elections and I made an analysis when I looked at the overall electoral body and I saw that the HDZ actually won 32 per cent approximately of the electoral body as a whole -- I mean the electoral body of Croatia -- and the HDZ approximately 24 per cent of the total number of voters in Croatia. I think Smiljko Sokol had prepared all of this and, on one occasion, he even said that this law of his was revenge on communism. So, in the final outcome, the HDZ had almost an absolute majority in the Croat Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us something about the reorganisation of the secretariat for the interior on the territory of the city and municipality of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Secretariat of Internal Affairs in Croatia is organised according to municipalities, that is to say, that there was a Republican Secretariat and there were Municipal Secretariats of Internal Affairs in all the municipalities in Croatia. Some time before the elections, I think that this was during 1989, there was a reorganisation of this secretariat. It went along the following lines: instead of being organised according to municipalities, it was organised in a smaller number of secretariats at the level of the entire republic and this resulted in the following -- in the municipality of Vukovar, the Secretariat for the Interior was abolished and there was one for the entire territory of Vinkovci, Zupanja and Vukovar. Until then, there was this kind of secretariat in Vukovar, so that Secretary for Internal Affairs -- at that time it was Mr. Lodinovic, who was directly responsible to the Republican Secretariat for Internal Affairs, but also, horizontally, he was responsible to the Assembly of the Municipality of Vukovar and he had to submit his reports to him and that is what the Assembly did, as a rule, every year. When this new secretariat was constituted for the territory of all three municipalities, the Assembly of the Municipality of Vukovar lost all jurisdiction, so to speak, over this Secretariat for Internal Affairs. As I said, this happened even before the elections and it caused quite a bit of dissatisfaction. It stirred up quite a tempest, because the people felt equal before, but when the Municipality of Vukovar was supposed to melt into Vinkovski and Zupanja that had a Croat majority population, they thought that they were losing ground. Mr. Lodinovic was secretary at the time, although I remember that Mr. Dokmanovic was held responsible by some people for having let this happen, but at that time he was not President of the municipality at all. At any rate, this reorganisation was carried out by the Secretariat for Internal Affairs, and the result was that some 40 professionals -- perhaps I should mention before that that the Secretariat of Internal Affairs of Vukovar is part of the overall Republican Secretariat and was often recognised as a very well professionally organised department and they had some very good professionals on their staff, and about 40 professionals from the secretariat received orders that they would no longer be employed in Vukovar but in Vinkovski -- most of these people were Serbs and of course this was not met with enthusiasm. On the contrary, it was taken as punishment and even worse than that. When the possibility was provided for their premature retirement, about 25 of these professionals from that secretariat retired prematurely. Among them was my cousin, Bogdan Krnajac, who was, for many years, head of the Department for General Affairs, so I know this from the horse's mouth, and I was also a good friend of Mr. Lodinovic's, and I would come to the secretariat quite often while he was there and often afterwards when Mr. Sredoselac came to head the secretariat, too. At any rate, this reorganisation which started before the elections continued after the elections, too. After the elections, the Municipal Assembly did not have any jurisdiction whatsoever over this secretariat, because there was now a single secretariat for all three municipalities and at the level of Vukovar itself there was only a police station, and this police station was headed by a Croat, Mr. Sredoselac. Until then, there were about 200 people who were employed there -- I do not know if Serbs or Croats were a majority, but an effort was made to have more or less equal representation. So, after the reorganisation, there was a drastic change. I said already that, due to the fact that they were transferred to Vinkovski, many of these professionals retired prematurely, so new people were taken according to the information that I received I would come to see them quite often and these individuals were ethnic Croats exclusively. In the meantime, the Secretariat for Internal Affairs was transformed into a Ministry of the Interior -- it was called the MUP and, by May, it had 700 people, and already then, as the Serbs left the police, it became an uni-ethnic force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether we could take a break now, but I suggest, and I hope the interpreters will not be angry at me, that we have only a 15 minute recess, so at 12 o'clock sharp we should resume. (11.45 a.m.). (A short break). (12 noon).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us, briefly, about how the Croat Parliament was constituted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the elections, the Parliament was constituted, the mandates of the elected members were verified, I remember that there was quite a bit of pomp involved when the Parliament was constituted. I remember the euphoria in front of the Parliament building itself and this first day of Parliament was quite euphoric altogether -- the atmosphere was euphoric. It was a very formal occasion, so we did not actually start with our work -- it was ceremonial -- but, at the very outset, I got this impression that there was such a lot of euphoria and intolerance involved, and when I saw the expressions on all the faces of these people who were representatives, who were Members of Parliament, I realised that this did no really auger well for the future. I crossed the street from the Parliament building -- I walked across the square to the former head of the Croat parliamentary delegation to the Assembly of Yugoslavia, to Mr. Skakic. He is a relative of mine, he is my uncle. I told him about my fears, that all of this did not auger well. He was quite upset, too, but he assured me that all would be well after all. However, at the very outset of our work, it became obvious that he was not right -- at the first working session already, there was a discussion about replacing three directors -- Serbs -- who were directors of major public enterprises, public companies -- I remember that the Director of Television was amongst them. The representatives of the SDP, especially were very dissatisfied by this. One of the members asked for this item to be removed from the agenda, because this would cause even more ethnic intolerance, but Mr. Dokmanovic, the presiding person in the Parliament, said that this could not be so because the HDZ was a democratic Party and they had the legitimate right of representing exclusively the interests of all the people of Croatia, all the citizens of Croatia and that this was their right only because they had won an absolute majority. I asked for the floor. I had prepared an analysis of the results of the elections, and I wanted to refute the statement that had just been made by the President of the Parliament by resorting to facts, because official analysis showed that only 32 per cent of the electorate had voted for the HDZ and that they, by no means, had the exclusive right to represent the interests of the people of Croatia. When Mr. Domljan realised what I was about to say, he said that he would take the floor away from me. After that, he actually did take the floor away from me. He would not let me speak, because obviously he did not want the results of the elections to be heard from that point of view. The work of the Parliament continued, because, in fact, since the HDZ had an absolute majority, the atmosphere was very bad, very intolerant, very unpleasant, because whenever anybody said something from the rostrum that was not in line with what the HDZ members thought, they would boo this person, and, also, I remember that the son of General Bobetko, who was an MP then, I remember he threw his bag at the rostrum, when another member of Parliament was speaking, and he did not like the views that were presented by this person .

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think it would be interesting for us to hear about the constitutional changes that took place in Croatia then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this kind of atmosphere, as the work of the Parliament progressed, there was a debate on changing the constitution of Croatia and a public debate was initiated on the adoption of a new constitution. This created havoc throughout Croatia, because Serbs were no longer to be a constituent element of the Croat State; they were to be turned into a national minority. This caused major dissatisfaction, and a lack of confidence in this same Government, especially amongst the Serbs, but regardless of this proposal, we tried within the SDP Party itself and, when we realised that they defended this position with not very many arguments, that is, this position that Croatia should not be organised as a national State but as a State of citizens, then the four of us, members of Parliament from Vukovar, took our distance from the SDP of Mr. Racan and a debate was conducted not only by us as members of Parliament, but also from the Municipal Assembly itself. We gave certain proposals which were aimed at reaching a compromise, so that the State could be constituted as a State of citizens, not a national State, and also we had another series of amendments, which were again aimed at compromise. On the one hand, there was the view of the Government of the HDZ and, on the other hand, it was that which was acceptable to the Serbs: there were quite a few discussions and meeting devoted to this particular subject matter, and little by little there was increasing polarisation -- many Croats did not agree with the positions of the HDZ but they would not present their own views. The Serbs who presented their views had no way of presenting their views, except through us -- their MPs -- and, gradually, we had -- enjoyed less and less confidence among the citizens, because they were increasingly unsatisfied. After the debate in Parliament where amendments were discussed, not a single one of these amendments was accepted. In the Parliament there was a voting machinery, and it was in favour of the Government proposal, which was adopted in its entirety. I believe that this was a key breaking point in this effort to create a greater understanding and confidence between the different ethnic groups. I was convinced that Croatia could have had Serbs as loyal citizens within their State, had they only shown more tolerance and more patience. After this constitution was adopted, it became clear to me that this chance was gambled away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You also have some interesting information as regards the composition of the Parliament and Government in terms of the sentences that were pronounced on these people beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The intention of the Parliament was to publish a book -- an expensive glossy publication and all of us members of Parliament were supposed to write our CVs. It was virtually impossible to have a democratic discussion at the meetings of Parliament themselves, because the atmosphere was not really conducive to that. So, sometimes we would go into other rooms in the Parliament and I had a look at all the CVs and I realised that most of the MPs, instead of starting their CVs by saying, "I was born in such and such a place at such and such a date," they started out by saying, "I had spent such and such a number of years in prison" et cetera and I realised that there were quite a few of them who did that, and that is why I -- it is only then that I realised why there was such a degree of intolerance at that particular meeting and at other meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I suggest we now go back to the town of Vukovar itself and the municipality of Vukovar. The election of the new authorities in Vukovar after the first multi-Party elections --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you of the results of the election -- the SDP, from its list, won more than a two-third majority amongst the delegates for the Municipal Assembly, and, when they were constituted, the discussion held within the Party as to how to distribute the functions in the Municipal Assembly, I was convinced that we should show goodwill to the HDZ and to offer more posts than they would have got by virtue of the votes won. My proposal was accepted and the HDZ was asked to provide candidates for the Vice-President of the Municipal Assembly and for the President of one Chamber and the Vice-President of two Chambers. Although these were a greater number of posts than the HDZ should have been allotted as the Vukovar municipality was a multi-nationality community where the dominant nations were the Serb and Croat, it was standard practice that if, for the President of the Municipal Assembly, a Serb is elected, then the President of the Executive Council, which is the location of executive power, be a Croat and vice versa. That was the principle applied. So, although there was a large measure of goodwill shown on our part, the HDZ showed a high degree of intolerance and it was not satisfied with the results of the elections; it was dissatisfied because, as a Party, they did not come into power in the municipality and from the start they began to obstruct the work of the Municipal Assembly and made it difficult to elect the President and the President of the council and, when discussing the Rules of Procedure, they asked that the Rules of Procedure be amended and it was, according to the rules, only if the general interest came into play that decision-making was done by a two-thirds majority. They insisted that all questions be decided upon by a two-thirds majority, so as to make the work of the Municipal Assembly more difficult. It is my personal impression that this was a systematic obstruction and that everything was done to make life very difficult and that the delegate and the President of the Municipal Assembly, a high degree of tolerance was shown, so that a democratic atmosphere may prevail and that decisions be in keeping with the Rules of Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you -- we are going to discuss the elections of the President of the Municipal Assembly -- to tell us what list was Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic elected as President of the Municipal Assembly -- what list was he on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a candidate of the SDP Party -- the Party of Democratic Change. We put forward two candidates on behalf of our Party and then the Assembly was to decide. The second candidate was Mrs. Peter -- the election was done by secret ballot and, as far as I recall, Mr. Dokmanovic won two-thirds of the vote and Mrs. Peter won one-third of the vote. The elections took place in keeping with the Rules of Procedure. We provided two candidates, and the deputies elected Mr. Dokmanovic, who was appointed President of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the work of the Municipal Assembly itself, particularly at this time of national tension in the Vukovar region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly did not have executive powers, but, rather, it had the task of coordinating matters, of solving problems of common interest to the municipality and the President of the municipality had the task of chairing the meetings. Executive power lay in the Executive Council led by the President of the Executive Council. As I say, from the very start, work was made very difficult, because of the obstructions made by the SDP and Mr. Mercep was very intolerant, he was insulting on many occasions, and made life very difficult. He called various individuals thieves, all those who had held power and authority positions earlier on -- he called them -- abused them and so on -- insulted them. This contributed to the creation of tension. On the other hand, the Party for Democratic Change asked that problems be solved through political dialogue. Mr. Dokmanovic, as President, showed a lot of goodwill in this regard. He tried to ensure a democratic atmosphere for the work of the Assembly. I am not quite sure whether Mr. Dokmanovic was a member of the SDP at the time, but he was on the SDP's list, as was the other candidate, as we had gained a two-thirds majority, and therefore it was up to the Party to nominate two candidates. As I say, life was made fairly difficult, but we did manage to function more or less according to the Rules of Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the endeavours of the President of the Municipal Assembly, Slavko Dokmanovic, to deal with the problems that were burgeoning from one day to the next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall one particular detail where seven or eight villages from the municipality of Vinkovski-- where there was a majority Serb population -- they brought in a decision and tabled a demand to the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar requesting that they come under the competence of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar, that is, to be incorporated into the Vukovar municipality. Mr. Dokmanovic explained the position and said that, under the prevailing conditions, this would not be a good idea, and did not accept this initiative on the part of the villages and so this was not placed on the agenda of the Assembly's discussions. There were several other cases where a compromise solution was sought, which would be acceptable to one and all, including the HDZ. Unfortunately, this did not meet with understanding from the other side, and there were frequent attempts at seizing power in the municipality and, at one point, I think that this was deputy Fekete, proposed that a vote of confidence be voted for Mr. Dokmanovic. This initiative was accepted, and they became aware of the fact that, democratically, they would not be able to assume power and that the Municipal Assembly was, in fact, functioning according to the Rules of Procedure and that, therefore, it would be very difficult to change the power structure in their favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the effect in some circles -- what effect did these endeavours of the President of the assembly have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, when the Serbs in Croatia gradually became to lose their confidence in the newly elected authorities, all those who tried democratically and in a tolerant manner through dialogue to seek compromise solutions with the representatives of the Croat authorities, for the most part they began losing their authority. Mr. Dokmanovic's attempts to find democratic and compromise solutions and to arrive at generally acceptable ones led, as a consequence, to the fact that he lost his authority with the Serbs. That happened with me as well, and all those who attempted, precisely because there was a lot of reason for dissatisfaction among the Serbs, sought peaceful democratic solutions in negotiations with the Municipal Authorities. What happened was that certain Serbs and some deputies would criticise Mr. Dokmanovic during meetings. They said that he was not radical enough and that they found his efforts unacceptable -- his efforts at solving matters democratically unacceptable because they were not proving fruitful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The contacts that the President Dokmanovic had with the Prime Minister also had negative reactions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not only with him. We had talked very frequently. We took part together in solving problems. Mr. Dokmanovic and myself spent a lot of time in my own home trying to find compromise solutions to the newly arisen situation -- at least peaceful solutions -- but these come upon dissatisfaction among the Serbs, because their own dissatisfaction was mounting and so were their own fears, and they were of the opinion that it was our fault for not taking a sharp enough stand in defending Serb interests in Croatia, because we had agreed to discuss matters with all representatives of the Republican authorities, and on many occasions Mr. Dokmanovic and myself discussed matters with Mr. Degoricija and other representatives of the Republican authorities -- Mr. Dokmanovic also had talks with Mr. Mesic when he came to open a road around Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the time, he was the Prime Minister of Croatia, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was the case but, at all events, these contacts were very frequent, but precisely because the Republican authorities gave too many arguments to nurture Serb dissatisfaction, Mr. Dokmanovic and myself lost the confidence that the Serbs had placed in us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In going about your daily duties, that is to say, when you went to work, when Mr. Dokmanovic went to work in the Municipal Assembly building, did he have any problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, tensions grew gradually. In the course of 1990, they were not at their peak yet, but they could be felt. The crux came with the adoption of the constitution on the proposal of the Government of Croatia and the next breakdown came after the word Plitvice excesses, when there was very marked fear on the part of the Serbs and especially when barricades were set up in the villages populated by the Serbs. Up until then, Mr. Dokmanovic was able to go to work normally, but, before 1 May, at some point before 1 May, he was not able to go to work normally. He did not dare. Afterwards, he would go to his office in the Municipal Assembly building only by official car. When I went to Trpinja when I went to fetch him by car, because he thought he could count on me and that the people would not shoot at me, because there were threats to liquidate him, and that is how he went to work. I went to fetch him in an official car. I recall one occasion when Mr. Josko Moric came --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Josko Moric please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Josko Moric was a high functionary in the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We sat down for talks together in Mr. Dokmanovic's office. He had had threats that, on the road from Trpinja to Vukovar, he would be ambushed and liquidated. He himself told me that he had very frequent -- his official car was frequently searched, although he was commonly known as "mayor" and I myself know that on many occasions he was met by police officers and asked to leave the car. He said he was the mayor, the President of the Municipal Assembly, but this did not help.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: These were representatives of the Croat MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they would make him leave the car and they would search him for weapons, for example. He would have to place his hands up on the car and he would be searched. All this was highly degrading and was conceived to create this psychosis of fear and these threats contributed to that fear. I think, on several occasions, he had to reach his office in a transporter. I recall that, on one occasion, he called me at my office in the PTT building where I was at work -- he called me from Mr. Gorsic's house -- and he asked me to come quickly because he had been told that an ambush had been set up and that we should organise his flee from Vukovar and we called out a garrison vehicle to transport him. So that, after 2 May, when the well-known events took place in Borovo Selo, he did not dare to go to work except when we could provide all the necessary security arrangements whereby he could go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When was the last session of the Assembly and was it held, or was it only scheduled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As members of the Assembly, we were supposed to coordinate the work of the Municipal Assembly. We were not full members in terms of decision-making, but we were supposed to coordinate their work with the Croat Parliament. So, regularly, whenever I was not attending sessions of the Croat Parliament, I would take part in the work of the Municipal Assembly. I think that the last session was some time before May, and it was scheduled for mid May. However, that particular session was not held, because armed persons and individuals from the HDZ did not allow this session to be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you know how this particular Municipal Assembly, in which Slavko Dokmanovic was a deputy and whose President he was, ended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic could not work normally as President of the Assembly after the incident in Borovo Selo and the work of the Municipal Assembly itself practically stopped because this session was prevented from taking place by these armed members of the HDZ and other armed individuals, so this was not held and it seems to me that at the end of that month, that by a decree --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sorry, what month, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was the end of June, if I am not mistaken -- no, no, sorry -- some time in June -- I am not sure any more, because in May the session was not held, so it might have been the beginning of June -- I am not really too sure any more. Well, a decree was passed by the Government of Croatia, the Minister of the Judiciary had signed it -- and thus the Municipal Assembly was dissolved and a representative of the Government of Croatia was thus appointed and, in fact, in the authorities of the municipality --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sorry, that was not translated, according to the transcript, what exact month this was in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure whether I said it was the end of June -- I am not sure, but I think it was the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very briefly, could you give us an assessment of the work of Slavko Dokmanovic as President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar while he held that office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a Party, when we were to decide who our candidates for the post of President of the Municipal Assembly would be, we sought to find people who enjoyed the confidence of the people in the municipality, and who were moderate, and it is according to these criteria that Mrs. Peter and Mr. Dokmanovic were proposed, so he was proposed by the Party as a person who enjoyed a reputation within the municipality and whose ideas and behaviour were moderate. So these traits of his, while he was a candidate of ours, were retained throughout his tenure of office. He always tried to find a solution by peaceful political means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to a different subject. If you agree, this should be a bit more concise, that is to say, we would like to see how an armed conflict broke out later -- the incident in Plitvice, the spring of 1991 -- March, I believe. Tell us briefly who the protagonists were and what were the consequences of that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This happened some time in the spring -- I think it was end of March or beginning of April, or some time around that period. I do not know exactly why Mr. Hadzic and Mr. Savic were at Plitvice then, whether they were coming or going to or from a meeting of the Serb National Council, I am not sure about that, but, at any rate, there was an armed intervention by the forces of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia; the two of them were arrested; they were taken to prison in Zagreb, and this piece of news resounded throughout the municipality of Vukovar and it only contributed to this climate of distrust and people became even more fearful, and since they lost all confidence in the republican authorities, they sought ways and means of continuing their existence. I remember that I thought at the time that this would cause major trouble, and I insisted, with Racan and others, particularly Mr. Degoricija, that the two arrested persons be released as soon as possible, and, if necessary, that they be tried before a court of law, but that they should be released, because this would lead to unforeseeable consequences and that this could even create a situation which would be conducive to civil war. At our major insistence this was done after a few days, but just to give you a detail, showing the extent of distrust this kind of behaviour of the Republican Government created among the people and also we were losing confidence among the Serbs in the municipality, all of us who were advocating peaceful solutions -- and I include both Mr. Dokmanovic and myself among these people -- I tried to assure Mr. Hadzic's sister that they would be released and I was told in insulting terms that I was an traitor and that Mr. Dokmanovic and I did not sufficiently represent the interests of the Serbs and that we were not needed by the Serbs of the municipality as such. At any rate, this truly had unforeseeable consequences, particularly at first. Road blocks were set up in Borovo Selo, mostly consisting of agricultural machinery and other obstacles and people stayed primarily in those villages where there was a predominantly Serb population, and, as I said, this, in my opinion, was one of the major turning points -- I am not saying that Borovo Selo was already civil war but it certainly contributed to it. As far as Mr. Dokmanovic is concerned, I tried to pacify the situation -- already, at that stage, I asked people who had held posts of responsibility in the Croat Government and in the Parliament to come to the municipality of Vukovar and if they did not trust me and Mr. Dokmanovic, that they should address the deputies in the Municipal Assembly themselves. Mr. Degoricija accepted this and he came. Mr. Bogdanic also came, another Member of Parliament and we tried to explain to the deputies in the Municipal Assembly that the Government of the Republic of Croatia would behave according to the law and that it would not create a climate of distrust, but they did not believe us or Mr. Degoricija because of everything that had happened. All in all, this created a feeling, a climate, of exceptional mistrust and, when we tried to pacify the situation through our own activities, usually some kind of action taken by the police beyond our control jeopardised all of that. I tried to convince Mr. Soskocanin from Borovo Selo, for example, that he should meet with Mr. Sredoselac, chief of the police station in Vukovar, and we came to Borovo Selo, and we talked to Mr. Soskocanin, and we sought a solution as to how the road blocks could be removed and how traffic could be re-established and this was indeed achieved. It was late in the evening and already the next day a police car that was moving through Borovo Selo was shot at, so, after all the painstaking efforts we took, this one single action put all this down the drain. I told Mr. Soskocanin about it -- I objected and he said they were not his people, although they were wearing police uniforms and he was officially head of the police station, and he was supposed to have all the policemen in that area under his control. There were also other cases where we tried and succeeded in the short run to find a compromising solution and we calmed the situation down, but soon similar action would follow and then everything went down the drain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You are referring to the action in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to the action in Plitvice, too, but what was particularly obvious was almost on a regular basis, before sessions of Parliament, there would be some excessive situations and this certainly could not be by accident altogether. In Krajina, when road blocks were put, this was yet another provocation before the session of the Assembly, so this action was provoked by other behaviour, as was the situation in Plitvice and also in Borovo Selo. My personal impression is that these situations were provoked, so the Serbs could be accused as the culprits, and that this was a premeditated effort to have a homogenised national feeling and there was an organised effort involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was there organised arming in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not see weapons distributed, but, on several occasions, I heard such information in the Municipal Assembly and, on a few occasions, in passing, I received such information, that arms were being distributed to HDZ members, even by HDZ deputies from the Assembly, but in the Croat Parliament itself, people discussed this rather openly, and certain individuals from the HDZ boasted about it saying that the HDZ members were being armed. All of this was at the end of 1990 and beginning of 1991 and nothing was concealed by May -- in May people spoke of it quite openly. I remember that a member of the Municipal Assembly put a question at the session of the Municipal Assembly itself -- could somebody please explain to him why weapons were being distributed, because in broad daylight, he said that he witnessed the distribution of weapons to civilians from a truck and he did not want to comment on this and no-one wanted to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who is Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tomislav Mercep was head of the HDZ in the municipality of Vukovar and in fact he led the activities of that Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us about his activities in the territory of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually met Mercep at the pre-election meeting in Lovas. I did not know about him before that, although for many years I was Director of the PTT, and I knew more or less all prominent citizens in the municipality, but I did not know him, and I did not know all others who were in that Party, either. From the very moment I met him at this pre-election meeting, he showed a high degree of intolerance and, very often at sessions of the Assembly itself he spoke very insultingly of others, calling them thieves, liars, and the like, and I remember, once, Mr. Degoricija was present, too -- this meeting was being held in the castle of Count --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Could you clarify who Mr. Degoricija was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Degoricija was Deputy Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, and it was his job to coordinate the work with the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar and he was President of the Municipal -- the Chamber in which I worked, too. We tried and Mr. Degoricija came for this purpose, to calm the situation down, and to make matters a little easier, but at that meeting as well, Mr. Mercep was very arrogant and aggressive, he called everybody else a thief. I asked for the floor and said that to say somebody was a thief without arguments was not only uncivilised, but that it spoke more about the person who had uttered these insults than the person whom they were directed at. Mr. Degoricija said that he had gone too far and he calmed him down. But he was exceptionally dissatisfied with the fact that they had not won over power and authority in the municipality in Vukovar and, through his activities, tried to gain power, or sabotage the work of others. When they were not given a vote of confidence in having Mr. Dokmanovic step down, he said that he would gain power forcibly. I shall later tell you of the events that took place afterwards when they stepped far out of the realm of politics and entered a completely different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, of how power was taken over -- how Radio Vukovar was taken over or control of the local police was assumed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they did not succeed legally through legal means in replacing the authorities in the municipality, they tried and succeeded in using force and Radio Vukovar, which was held by people working professionally in the Radio, when they were forcibly replaced, and made to leave the building. Mr. Mercep did this and his associates, and they appointed other individuals -- a similar thing happened in the National Defence and the secretary was forcibly thrown out of his offices and Mr. Mercep and his associates took over. I do not know whether he had any documents allowing him to do so, but he did assume this function, and the Municipal Assembly made no decision in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: From your statement, we see a rather bizarre detail. When you went to Mr. Mercep, to his house for a meeting, something rather bizarre happened. Could you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This event took place when, after many organised meetings outside the work of the Municipal Assembly, when the political parties met, we would hold discussions until late at night -- we discussed the problems that had occurred and we had found compromise solutions and we were then to write the minutes of that meeting. It was very late on that particular occasion and we decided that we would come early tomorrow morning to Mrs. Peter, Mr. Mercep and myself and to write down the minutes of the meeting. Mrs. Peter said that she could not come early, because she had already had some work with her chickens, she was going to slaughter some of her chickens that day. Mr. Modalek -- he was also deputy in the Parliament -- said we would come and help. Mercep's comment was that he would not be able to be present because he could not stand the sight of chickens being slaughtered. He always liked a good joke. Mr. Modalek said, "Never mind, I will put the sajkaca cap on their heads." Mercep said, "then There is no problem, I will slaughter them myself." That was a very bizarre joke -- unpalatable -- but all this demonstrated the great difficulties -- we had to have democratic and constructive dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Would you explain what this "sajkaca" cap means; what does the sajkaca symbolise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The sajkaca is the national cap worn by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was the head of the hospital in Vukovar also replaced on that occasion -- he was a Serb by nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Croatia, I said that there were many Serb directors of large enterprises, and their replacements started hand-in-hand with a legal regulation from the Assembly, which moved towards the centralisation of all public enterprises -- in order to be able to manage them better from one centre, so this was done with the PTT, post, telegraph and telephone service and by decree of the SABOR or Parliament, a public enterprise for the PTT was set up, and the post activities were separated from the telecommunication activities and all the present directors were relieved of their duties, and at all levels, so in the post section and in the telecommunications section, new people were appointed to these posts. As director of the PTT of Vukovar, I was relieved of my duties. Later on, the manager, that is to say, of a lower rank for the units, without any actual authorisation or competencies in my work, which meant that full centralisation for public enterprises had taken place, and all the directors had been replaced -- all the Serb directors of the public enterprises were replaced in the municipality itself -- and this happened from May onwards, when Mercep in fact took over the complete command of the town. It is my impression at the time that neither the police -- that the commander of the police station of Vukovar, Mr. Sredoselac and later on his replacement, somebody else was appointed, but they had no power and authority over the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who replaced the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Croats were placed in the positions that were held by the Serbs -- the director of the hospital was a Serb, he was replaced. I do not know whether Mr. Gavro came first and then Mr. Bosanac, but he was replaced as the director of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I should now like to go on to the events which represent a turning point for Vukovar -- 1 and 2 May. What happened on 1 May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1 May was always traditionally celebrated by the fact that citizens went to the environs of Vukovar near Borovo Selo and Sumadica, which was closer to the town centre. It was my intention that, despite the very difficult situation, to take my family out for an outing in celebration of 1 May, but there were certain excessive situations, and a senior citizen, a Serb by nationality, was killed by another elderly gentleman of the Croat nationality -- I think he was part Croat and part Hungarian. I called the crisis headquarters in the village to ask what had happened, what was going on, and went by car, as I did previously -- whenever there was a situation -- an excessive situation of this kind, I would personally go on the spot in the locality to try and calm the citizens -- the people, to reduce tensions. That is what I did on this particular occasion as well. The villagers, who were very angry at this murder, this killing, had surrounded the house of the individual who had done the shooting and killed the man. I talked to the people in the local community and in the crisis headquarters as it was referred to, and asked that calm prevail. I know that Savo Davidovic who was from that particular village and is also a deputy and myself, I think that Mr. Bosnjakovic was with me and he was also a deputy, a representative -- we tried to calm the situation, and finally I did succeed in allowing the police to take Mr. Gelencin away, because the police maintained that it would have an on-the-site investigation, and that this would come up before the courts in due course. Unfortunately, as happened on many previous occasions this was not done because Mr. Gelencin was never taken to court. So, all in all, this resulted in a further loss of authority, both my own authority and everything else -- everybody else, including Mr. Dokmanovic, because we all tried to deal with the problem peaceably. I went back to the police station that same day, where I came across Mr. Sredoselac and Mr. Markovic was there -- he was a member of the special MUP Croat forces, and for some 10 days he was in the police station at Vukovar, and as I was at the police station practically every day, whenever some excessive events took place where Serbs were involved, they would inform me and I would go there and see what was going on and try to calm the situation and, when the Serb population came to me to intervene, then I would do the same. So, I met these two individuals, and, once again, for the umpteenth time, I tried to explain that we should refrain from the use of force, because with a people who, from the first day, were peaceable -- and I can say this with my full conviction -- they were already to solve things peaceably and always ready for dialogue, but the people began to use patience and confidence and fear started to set in. The development of events led to an escalation of fear and led to a readiness to protect one's own existence and one's family by using other means. I always warned them and cautioned them not to take up arms. I remember that Mr. Markovic said to me that I should agree that they apply force. It was only up to me to agree and he said that then they would clear matters up. I think I spent some two hours late at night discussing this problem, and I went home afterwards, and I asked an on-the-spot investigation to be conducted, and for reports to be submitted so we could show the Serbs that the police were doing something in that particular situation. But, they told us that it was late and that an on-the-spot investigation could not be conducted, but that it would be conducted the following day. On the following day, which was 2 May, I went to the PTT building -- I think it was around 10 o'clock -- they called me from the police station and said that an investigating judge from the court in Osijek arrived. I think this was then under the competence of the court in Osijek, but that he did not dare go on the spot to make his investigation, because people from the local community had said that they would not admit any policeman into the village, because they had some very bad experiences, and that there was rifle fire on the part of the uniformed individuals. I intervened, I asked them -- I told them that I would be responsible and then they agreed, and so, with a group of journalists, who asked to go with me, went together with a police car and two policemen and the investigating judge -- we went to the village and held initial talks in the local community and then, an on-the-spot investigation was conducted by the judge. I remember that one of the sons of the gentleman who was killed was there. The atmosphere was a correct one and they made their statements and said how this event came about. The judge finished his investigation quickly and he said that he would be leaving with the policemen. This was already at the very outskirts of the village towards Vukovar -- 500 or 600 metres away from this forest (INAUDIBLE) left and I remained to talk to the people in the village and the journalists remained, too. At one point, we heard shots from the direction of the forest. I came with my own private car, so I got into the car and I went to the forest straight away to see what was going on. The forest was on the right-hand side and on the left-hand side were silos, with wheat, and there were snipers of the Croat MUP on the silos and on the road in front of the forest there were three vehicles -- a Renault traffic and two Land Rovers. In each vehicle there were 8 fully armed policemen respectively, but I still did not link this with that which would happen afterwards. I asked what all of what was about. They said that somebody had shot from the direction of the forest and I said that they could pass freely, because I was there, and I went back to collect the journalist and, as I passed the forest and as I was approaching the outskirts of Vukovar, I met a large group of policemen. I stopped and I asked what all of that was about and they said that it was nothing special, that everything was fine, and I went on to the police station.
